term: 'Might makes right' (justice as the interest of the stronger)
beginner_explanation: The idea that there is no real justice beyond what benefits whoever is powerful enough to enforce their will.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, attributed by Plato to Thrasymachus and, in different terms, to Callicles, that justice is nothing but the advantage of the ruling power and that law and conventional morality are merely devices, invented either by rulers for their own benefit or by the weak to restrain the strong.

beginner_explanation: The final destination of Hegel's dialectic: pure thought thinking about itself, which Hegel treats as equivalent to God.
academic_explanation: The culminating category of Hegel's Logic, defined as the unity of the Subjective and Objective Idea -- thought whose only object is itself -- which Russell glosses as 'truly a Professor's God.'

beginner_explanation: The idea, developed within Plato's sceptical Academy, that even without certainty, some beliefs are more likely true than others and should guide action.
academic_explanation: The constructive doctrine, associated with Carneades and Clitomachus, that degrees of probability, though never amounting to certainty, provide a rational and sufficient basis for belief and practical action.

beginner_explanation: Any change in an object's speed or direction of motion -- not just speeding up, but also slowing down or turning.
academic_explanation: Change of velocity, whether in magnitude or direction; Galileo's key discovery in dynamics, later the quantity that Newton's laws of motion and gravitation are formulated to explain, and which Russell notes remains the basis of dynamical law even after the concept of 'force' was found dispensable.
related_concepts: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions
Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

beginner_explanation: The hilltop citadel of Athens and its most famous temple, both rebuilt under Pericles after being destroyed by the Persians.
academic_explanation: The religious and civic center of Athens, whose temples were burned by Xerxes's forces and subsequently rebuilt through Pericles's initiative, employing Pheidias, as the visible monument of Periclean wealth and ambition.

beginner_explanation: A 1534 English law declaring King Henry VIII, rather than the Pope, the head of the Church of England.
academic_explanation: The 1534 Act of the English Parliament establishing Henry VIII as Supreme Head of the Church of England; Thomas More's refusal to swear the accompanying Oath of Supremacy led to his conviction for treason (on disputed testimony) and execution in 1535.
related_concepts: The limits of humanist reform in the face of religious polarization

beginner_explanation: Origen's book defending Christianity against the pagan critic Celsus's attacks.
academic_explanation: Origen's point-by-point apologetic rebuttal of Celsus's lost anti-Christian treatise, notable for articulating the classic twofold (rational plus scriptural/miraculous) argument for Christian belief.

beginner_explanation: Plato's story of prisoners who mistake shadows on a cave wall for reality, used to explain the difference between ordinary opinion and true philosophical knowledge.
academic_explanation: Plato's extended simile representing the ascent from sense-perception and opinion (shadows, firelight) to intellectual knowledge of the Ideas and the Good (sunlight outside the cave).

beginner_explanation: A conflict over whether a pagan statue symbolizing Rome's military success should remain in the Roman Senate House.
academic_explanation: A recurring late fourth-century controversy over the presence of the pagan Altar and Statue of Victory in the Roman Senate House, contested between pagan senators led by Symmachus and Christian authorities led by Ambrose, finally resolved in favor of the Christians after Theodosius's victory over the usurper Eugenius in 394.

beginner_explanation: A statement that is true just because of what its words mean, like 'all bachelors are unmarried.'
academic_explanation: In Leibniz, a proposition in which the predicate is contained in the notion of the subject; the basis of both the law of contradiction and, in his esoteric philosophy, the law of sufficient reason.

beginner_explanation: Plato's idea that learning is really just 'remembering' knowledge the soul had before it was born.
academic_explanation: The doctrine that a priori knowledge, especially mathematical and logical concepts not derivable from sense experience, is recollected from a prior, disembodied existence of the soul.

beginner_explanation: A pair of arguments that seem to both prove opposite conclusions, arising when you try to reason about the universe as a whole.
academic_explanation: Kant's term for the four pairs of thesis-and-antithesis arguments that arise from illegitimately applying space, time, or the categories beyond possible experience; influenced Hegel's dialectical method.

beginner_explanation: Jewish religious writings from around the time of the Old and New Testaments that were not included in the official Hebrew Bible, such as Ecclesiasticus and the Book of Enoch.
academic_explanation: Bodies of Second Temple-period Jewish literature excluded from the Hebrew canon (Apocrypha, e.g., Ecclesiasticus, 1-4 Maccabees) or falsely attributed to ancient authorities (Pseudepigrapha, e.g., the Book of Enoch), important as evidence for the development of Jewish thought immediately before Christianity.

beginner_explanation: Plato's account of the speech Socrates gave in his own defense at his trial.
academic_explanation: Plato's dialogue purporting to record Socrates's defence speech at his trial in 399 B.C., treated by Russell as broadly historical in intent though not a verbatim transcript.

beginner_explanation: The one basic 'stuff' that a Milesian philosopher claimed everything else is made of and can turn back into.
academic_explanation: The Milesian concept of a single underlying material principle from which all other substances are derived by transformation; realized differently by Thales (water), Anaximander (the boundless), and Anaximenes (air).

beginner_explanation: The claim that because the soul has no parts, it can't be broken apart or destroyed the way composite things can.
academic_explanation: Plato's argument that dissolution presupposes composition, that the soul is simple and akin to the unchanging essences it contemplates, and is therefore indestructible.
related_concepts: The argument from the soul's simplicity

beginner_explanation: The belief, taught by the priest Arius, that Jesus the Son was created by God the Father and is therefore not fully equal to Him.
academic_explanation: The Christological position, associated with Arius, that the Son is not co-eternal with or equal in substance to the Father but was created by Him; condemned as heresy at the Council of Nicaea (325) though it retained significant imperial and popular support for decades afterward.

beginner_explanation: A rebel who already has enough to eat and so cannot be driven simply by hunger or material want; instead their discontent is metaphysical or cosmic, and often expressed as grand self-assertion or Satanism.
academic_explanation: Russell's category for a type of rebellious figure distinguished from the materially motivated peasant or proletarian rebel; the aristocratic rebel's conscious grievance is a critique of the government of the world itself, taking the form of Titanic cosmic self-assertion or, in the religiously inclined, Satanism.

beginner_explanation: The idea that our thoughts and ideas become linked together through habit and repeated experience, and that this linking explains most of mental life.
academic_explanation: Hartley's and Bentham's psychological doctrine that association of ideas with one another and with language is the basic mechanism of mind, intended to support a deterministic account of mental occurrences comparable to Pavlov's later conditioned reflex.

beginner_explanation: The belief, imported from Babylon, that the movement of stars and planets determines or predicts human events and fates.
academic_explanation: A body of divinatory doctrine transmitted to the Greek world from Babylonian ('Chaldean') priestly tradition after Alexander's conquests, entailing a form of cosmic determinism that Russell notes most Hellenistic thinkers, including many Stoics, held alongside an inconsistent belief in Fortune.

beginner_explanation: The smallest possible piece of matter, according to the atomists: something so small it cannot be physically split any further.
academic_explanation: In Leucippus and Democritus's theory, a physically (though not geometrically) indivisible, indestructible unit of matter, differing from other atoms only in shape and size, moving eternally through the void.

beginner_explanation: Epicurus's idea that falling atoms occasionally veer very slightly off their straight path for no determined reason, which lets new combinations of matter form and leaves room for free will.
academic_explanation: Epicurus's modification of Democritus's strictly deterministic atomism: an uncaused, indeterminate deviation ('swerve') in the otherwise uniform downward fall of atoms, introduced to permit collisions that generate the world and to preserve human free will against physical determinism.

beginner_explanation: A movement of thinkers, mostly outside the clergy, who followed Averroes's teaching that only an impersonal intellect (not the individual soul) survives death, thereby denying personal immortality.
academic_explanation: The philosophical current, influential especially among Franciscans and at the University of Paris in the thirteenth century, that adopted Averroes's interpretation of Aristotle on the unity and impersonality of the active intellect, provoking ecclesiastical condemnation.

beginner_explanation: The view, drawn from Averroes, that only an impersonal, shared intellect survives death -- meaning individual people do not have personal immortality.
academic_explanation: The thirteenth-century Parisian doctrine, attributed to Averroes's interpretation of Aristotle's De Anima, that intellect is numerically one and impersonal across all human beings, denying individual personal immortality; explicitly rejected by Aquinas in favor of individually distinct souls/intellects.
related_concepts: Individual human soul, intellect, and the rejection of Averroism

beginner_explanation: The period (roughly 1309-1377) when the popes lived in Avignon, France, rather than Rome, and were widely seen as politically dependent on the French crown.
academic_explanation: The period beginning with Clement V's 1309 relocation of the papal court to Avignon, during which successive popes were widely regarded as politically subservient to the French monarchy, weakening papal claims to universal authority.

beginner_explanation: The principle that if you keep halving a quantity, you will eventually get something smaller than any amount you name in advance.
academic_explanation: The principle (used in the method of exhaustion) that for any two quantities a > b, there exists some whole number n such that repeated halving of a, n times, yields a quantity smaller than b, guaranteeing convergence of polygonal approximations.
related_concepts: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)

beginner_explanation: Gregory the Great's guide to the duties and conduct expected of bishops.
academic_explanation: Gregory the Great's treatise of advice for bishops, hugely influential through the early Middle Ages, given to bishops at consecration under Charlemagne and translated into Anglo-Saxon by Alfred the Great.
related_concepts: Papal political authority under Gregory the Great

beginner_explanation: The line of philosophers, from Locke through Hume to Mill, who build modest conclusions carefully from lots of observed facts.
academic_explanation: Russell's label for the inductive, piecemeal philosophical method running from Locke through Berkeley, Hume, and J. S. Mill, characterized by drawing cautious conclusions from broad empirical surveys.

beginner_explanation: The idea that there is no single 'self' behind our thoughts and feelings -- just a constantly changing collection of individual perceptions.
academic_explanation: Hume's conclusion, from the absence of any impression of the self, that personal identity consists in nothing but 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions ... in a perpetual flux and movement.'

beginner_explanation: The simplified, larger-than-life image of Byron as a despairing, sinning, freedom-loving rebel that spread across Europe (especially the Continent) and shaped later thought, regardless of how accurately it reflected the real, more complicated man.
academic_explanation: Russell's distinction between Byron's actual psychology and the operative historical 'myth' made of him abroad, which Russell treats as the genuinely causal, historically important entity, independent of its fidelity to Byron's real character.

beginner_explanation: The political and religious successor to Mahomet who ruled the Islamic empire.
academic_explanation: The head of the Islamic state as 'successor' (khalifa) to the Prophet, holding both political authority and inherited religious prestige; nominally elective but soon hereditary within the Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties.

beginner_explanation: The castle where Emperor Henry IV waited barefoot for three days in the snow to beg Pope Gregory VII's forgiveness in 1077.
academic_explanation: The site of Henry IV's 1077 penitential submission to Gregory VII during the Investiture Controversy; though it appeared a papal triumph, Russell notes the victory proved illusory once Gregory discovered Henry's repentance was insincere.
related_concepts: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV

beginner_explanation: Descartes's method of trying to doubt absolutely everything possible -- the senses, one's own body, even math -- in order to find something so certain it cannot be doubted at all, and build knowledge back up from there.
academic_explanation: The methodical, hyperbolic doubt with which Descartes opens the Discourse on Method and the Meditations, extending from ordinary sensory skepticism through the dreaming argument to the hypothesis of an all-powerful deceiving demon capable of undermining even mathematical certainty, undertaken to identify an absolutely indubitable foundation for knowledge.

beginner_explanation: Kant's rule that you should only act in ways you'd be willing to have everyone act, as a universal law -- not because of the results, but because it's the rational, dutiful thing to do.
academic_explanation: An unconditional command of practical reason, contrasted with the conditional 'hypothetical imperative'; formulated as 'Act only according to a maxim by which you can at the same time will that it shall become a general law.'

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's list of the ten most basic kinds of thing a word can signify: substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, and affection.
academic_explanation: The classification, set out in Aristotle's Categories, of the fundamental kinds of predication, which Russell says is offered 'with no suggestion of any principle' governing why these ten and no others were chosen, and which he finds unclear as a philosophical notion.

beginner_explanation: A dualist religious movement, strongest in southern France, that believed the material world was created by an evil power and that true goodness belonged only to a separate spiritual God.
academic_explanation: A medieval dualist heresy, descended via the Bogomiles and Paulicians from Manichaean and Gnostic sources, holding matter to be inherently evil and rejecting the Old Testament creator-God in favor of a distinct, purely spiritual good God revealed in the New Testament; suppressed by the Albigensian Crusade (from 1209) and the Inquisition.

beginner_explanation: Monks living together in a shared community, with common meals, work, and worship, rather than alone.
academic_explanation: Communal monastic life founded by Pachomius (c. 315-320), without private property, which became the dominant form of Western monasticism, later refined by Saint Benedict's Rule.

beginner_explanation: In an early Pythagorean theory, a fire at the center of the universe that the earth and other planets orbit, always hidden from the inhabited world.
academic_explanation: The central body of Philolaus's Pythagorean cosmology, around which ten heavenly bodies (including earth and a hypothetical counter-earth) were held to revolve, with the earth's rotation keeping the Mediterranean world perpetually turned away from it.

beginner_explanation: A system of government in which different groups (e.g., a prince, nobles, and the people) share power and limit each other, preventing any one from dominating.
academic_explanation: The constitutional principle, set forth explicitly in Machiavelli's Discourses, that apportioning power among prince, nobles, and people so that each checks the others produces greater political stability -- a principle Russell traces forward to Montesquieu and eighteenth-century liberal constitutionalism.
related_concepts: The republican doctrine of the Discourses: checks and balances and the value of liberty

beginner_explanation: Splitting government into separate branches (like lawmaking and law-enforcing) so that no one part gets too much power.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, formulated by Locke and developed further by Montesquieu, that legislative, executive, and (later) judicial functions of government should be institutionally separated to prevent abuse of power.

beginner_explanation: The idea, which Bergson rejects, that continuous change (like a film made of separate still frames) can be fully captured by a series of distinct, static states.
academic_explanation: Bergson's pejorative label for the view, which he attributes to both intellect and mathematics, that change is constituted by a succession of static states; Russell defends a refined version of this view (an infinite series of states with no 'next' state) as adequate to represent continuous motion.

beginner_explanation: Descartes's proposed test for truth: if you can conceive something with total clarity and precision, it must be true.
academic_explanation: The criterion Descartes adopts, generalizing from the evident certainty of the cogito, that whatever is conceived clearly and distinctly is true; used to justify mathematics and, more cautiously, physics, though Russell criticizes it as an unexamined scholastic-style maxim rather than something itself subjected to Cartesian doubt.
related_concepts: The criterion of clear and distinct ideas

beginner_explanation: Latin for 'I think, therefore I am' -- Descartes's famous argument that the very fact you are thinking (even if only doubting) proves you exist.
academic_explanation: Descartes's foundational argument that the act of thinking (including doubting) cannot be doubted away without self-contradiction, since the doubting itself is an instance of thought, yielding certain knowledge of one's own existence as a thinking thing, at least for as long as the thinking continues.
related_concepts: The cogito ('I think, therefore I am')

beginner_explanation: Plato's proposal that guardians share spouses and children in common rather than having private families.
academic_explanation: Plato's proposal abolishing private marriage and parenthood among guardians, replacing it with state-arranged, eugenically manipulated mating festivals and communal child-rearing with no acknowledged biological parentage.

beginner_explanation: Able to exist together at the same time without contradiction.
academic_explanation: Leibniz's term for possible entities that can coexist without logical contradiction; the actual world is, in his esoteric writings, the largest group of compossible entities.

beginner_explanation: The natural drive every living thing has to keep existing and protect itself.
academic_explanation: Spinoza's principle that everything, insofar as it is in itself, endeavors to persevere in its own being; the root of the passions in Book III of the Ethics.

beginner_explanation: A movement holding that a General Council of the whole Church, not the Pope alone, has ultimate authority -- used to resolve the Great Schism.
academic_explanation: The theological-political movement, building on theories developed by Marsiglio of Padua and Occam, asserting that a General Council holds authority superior to any single pope; it successfully resolved the Great Schism at the Council of Constance (1414-18) but was ultimately defeated as a permanent constitutional check on papal power by 1448.
related_concepts: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty

beginner_explanation: The idea that a General Council of the Church, rather than the Pope alone, holds ultimate authority in matters of doctrine and Church governance.
academic_explanation: The theory, developed by Marsiglio of Padua and adopted in modified form by Occam, that supreme ecclesiastical authority (including the power to excommunicate and authoritatively interpret Scripture) belongs to a representative General Council rather than to the Pope alone.
related_concepts: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty

beginner_explanation: Saint Augustine's autobiography, describing his sinful youth and his conversion to Christianity.
academic_explanation: Augustine's autobiographical and philosophical work recounting his intellectual and spiritual development from youth through conversion, later imitated by Rousseau and Tolstoy, and containing (in Book XI) what Russell considers Augustine's best purely philosophical writing (treated in Chapter IV).

beginner_explanation: Boethius's book, written in prison while awaiting execution, in which the figure of Philosophy comforts him with arguments about true happiness, fortune, and the good.
academic_explanation: A prosimetric (alternating prose and verse) philosophical dialogue composed by Boethius in 524, purely Platonic in metaphysical content though read throughout the Middle Ages as an orthodox Christian work.

beginner_explanation: The simple fact that one kind of event has always, so far, been followed by another kind of event -- which, for Hume, is all that 'causation' really amounts to.
academic_explanation: Hume's reductive account of causation: the observed regularity of one type of event being followed or accompanied by another, without any further perceivable necessary connection.

beginner_explanation: The line of philosophers, from Descartes through Leibniz to Kant and Hegel, who build huge logical systems from just a few starting principles.
academic_explanation: Russell's label for the deductive, systematic philosophical method running from Descartes through Spinoza and Leibniz to Kant and Hegel, characterized by 'pyramiding' extensive conclusions on a small number of a priori principles.

beginner_explanation: Russell's term for the dangerous pride of believing human beings can reshape reality (including truth itself) entirely to their own will, with no facts left to humble them.
academic_explanation: Russell's diagnosis of a modern philosophical and cultural danger arising when the traditional check of 'stubborn facts' (truth as independent of human power) is removed, tracing the danger's philosophical origin to Fichte and its cultural expression to modern technological confidence.

beginner_explanation: The idea that an impersonal force keeps the universe's conflicts (like the sun's daily path) within fixed, orderly limits.
academic_explanation: Heraclitus's doctrine that 'strife is justice': cosmic conflict between opposites is bounded by an impersonal necessity (the Erinys) that prevents any element or force from permanently overstepping its measure, extending Anaximander's earlier concept of cosmic justice.

beginner_explanation: The idea that all human beings, not just members of one's own city or people, belong to a single moral community.
academic_explanation: The doctrine that moral concern and citizenship extend in principle to all mankind rather than being confined by city or ethnicity; emerges in practice under Alexander and is systematized in theory by the Stoics.

beginner_explanation: A major church meeting called by Constantine in 325 to settle the dispute over Arianism.
academic_explanation: The first ecumenical council, convened by Constantine to resolve the Arian controversy and establish a standard of orthodoxy, condemning Arius's doctrine by an overwhelming majority.

beginner_explanation: The idea that God made the universe from nothing at all, rather than shaping already-existing material.
academic_explanation: The Scriptural doctrine, defended by Augustine against Greek philosophy and Manichaeism, that God created substance itself and not merely order imposed on eternal matter.

beginner_explanation: The glorification of the exceptional, self-assertive individual who imposes his will on history.
academic_explanation: The romantic doctrine, developed by Carlyle and Nietzsche, that extends individualism into the passions and celebrates heroic self-assertion; Russell argues it is self-refuting because its general adoption leads to despotism.

beginner_explanation: Russell's description of Rome's relationship to Greek culture: Rome relied almost entirely on Greek achievements in art, philosophy, and science rather than inventing its own.
academic_explanation: Russell's characterization of the Roman intellectual and artistic tradition as substantially derivative of Greek models throughout its history, in contrast to Rome's genuinely original contributions in law, engineering, and military/administrative organization.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's assumed ideal citizen: a person of leisure who combines aristocratic manners with a love of learning and the arts.
academic_explanation: The implicit aim of Aristotle's educational and citizenship proposals -- production of a leisured class combining aristocratic mentality with cultivated taste -- which Russell traces historically from Periclean Athens through the Renaissance to its dissolution by modern democracy, industrialism, and popular education.
related_concepts: The State as natural and prior to the individual

beginner_explanation: A follower of Diogenes's philosophy of rejecting material comfort, social convention, and desire in order to be free from fortune's power over you; originally meant 'dog-like' because of Diogenes's deliberately shameless lifestyle.
academic_explanation: A member of the philosophical tradition founded by Antisthenes and exemplified by Diogenes of Sinope, holding that virtue and freedom are achieved through the rejection of conventional social, material, and religious attachments ('defacing the coinage' of accepted values).

beginner_explanation: The inner 'voice' or sign Socrates said warned him away from certain actions.
academic_explanation: The private oracular sign Socrates describes in the Apology as guiding him negatively since childhood, of disputed nature (conscience versus a literal voice).

beginner_explanation: An alliance of Greek city-states formed to fight Persia that Athens gradually turned into an empire it controlled and profited from.
academic_explanation: A naval alliance, led by Athens, constituted so that member states contributed ships or their cash equivalent; as most states chose payment, Athens converted the resulting revenue and naval dominance into effective imperial control over its nominal allies.

beginner_explanation: Plato's name (in effect) for the craftsman-God who orders pre-existing chaotic matter into the world, rather than creating it from nothing.
academic_explanation: The creative agent of the Timaeus who, being good, orders pre-existing disorderly matter according to an eternal pattern, without creating that matter ex nihilo.
related_concepts: Creation as ordering of pre-existing chaos

beginner_explanation: The difference between what people actually want (desired) and what they truly ought to want (desirable) -- two different questions that Mill's argument mistakenly treats as the same.
academic_explanation: Russell's terminological distinction used to expose the fallacy in J. S. Mill's argument for utilitarianism: 'visible' means capable of being seen (a capacity), while 'desirable' means what ought to be desired (a normative claim), so 'desired' cannot validly entail 'desirable.'
related_concepts: J. S. Mill's proof of utilitarianism

beginner_explanation: The generals of Alexander the Great who fought over and divided up his empire after his death.
academic_explanation: The rival Macedonian generals -- principally Ptolemy, Seleucus, and Antigonus -- whose dynasties partitioned Alexander's empire into the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, and Antigonid kingdoms after decades of civil war.

beginner_explanation: Plato's method of pure reasoning that, unlike mathematics, needs no unproven starting assumptions and leads directly to knowledge of the Ideas.
academic_explanation: The highest exercise of 'reason' in Plato's divided line, proceeding without hypotheses to unconditioned knowledge culminating in the Idea of the Good.
related_concepts: The divided line: Reason versus Understanding

beginner_explanation: Socrates's method of asking question after question until someone's beliefs contradict each other.
academic_explanation: A method of philosophical inquiry proceeding by question and answer, aimed at testing consistency and eliciting definitions, traced by Russell to Zeno of Elea and developed by Socrates.

beginner_explanation: A pattern of historical change in stages, where each stage produces tensions that push society into the next stage -- for Marx, feudalism to capitalism to Socialism.
academic_explanation: Marx's adaptation of Hegel's dialectical logic of historical development, substituting classes (landowner, industrial employer, wage-earner) for Hegel's nations as the vehicles of an inevitable, deterministic historical movement.

beginner_explanation: Marx's view that knowing the world is not passive observation but an active, practical process in which the knower and the world shape each other.
academic_explanation: Marx's reinterpretation of materialism, under Hegelian influence, holding that sensation is an interaction between subject and object rather than passive contemplation, and that truth is demonstrated in practice rather than by isolated theoretical reflection.

beginner_explanation: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel, scattered across the ancient world.
academic_explanation: The dispersion of Jewish populations beyond Judea/Palestine, especially following the Babylonian exile and subsequent conquests, notably including large, hellenized communities such as that of Alexandria.

beginner_explanation: The claim that a king's authority to rule comes directly from God, not from the people's consent.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, rejected by early liberalism, that monarchical authority derives from a God-given hereditary right rather than from popular consent or contract.

beginner_explanation: Four especially authoritative early Christian teachers: Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory the Great.
academic_explanation: The four figures traditionally recognized as the great teaching authorities of the early Western Church, whose combined influence, per Russell, 'fixed the mould into which the Church was shaped.'

beginner_explanation: The idea that learning is really just remembering things the soul already knew before birth.
academic_explanation: The theory, applied by Socrates to geometry in the Phaedo and Meno, that all knowledge is recollection by the soul of truths known in a prior existence.

beginner_explanation: Russell's term for Scepticism's real character: not humble uncertainty, but a confident assertion that knowledge is definitely impossible.
academic_explanation: Russell's characterization of ancient Pyrrhonist Scepticism as itself a dogmatic position -- asserting with confidence the universal negative claim that 'nobody knows, and nobody ever can know' -- as distinct from either scientific probabilism or open inquiry.

beginner_explanation: A forged ancient document, believed genuine for centuries, in which the Emperor Constantine supposedly gave the Pope control over Rome and the whole Western Empire.
academic_explanation: An eighth-century forgery attributed to Constantine, used to provide antique legal justification for the papacy's temporal sovereignty over the Papal States; accepted as authentic throughout the medieval period and exposed as a fabrication by Lorenzo Valla in 1439.
related_concepts: Substitution of the authority of the ancients for the authority of the Church

beginner_explanation: The idea that there can be one truth arrived at by reason (philosophy) and a separate truth arrived at by faith (theology), with the two kept apart rather than blended together.
academic_explanation: A doctrine, traced by Russell to thirteenth-century Averroists condemned by the Church, holding that philosophy should proceed by reason alone while theology is accepted on revelation, with faith's 'triumph' considered greatest precisely where a dogma appears most absurd to unaided reason; Bacon advocated a version of this position, and Bayle later used it ironically.
related_concepts: The doctrine of 'double truth': separating philosophy from theology

beginner_explanation: Bergson's term for real, lived time, in which past experiences blend into the present rather than sitting in separate, measurable moments.
academic_explanation: Bergson's technical concept of 'pure duration' as the form conscious states take when the ego 'lets itself live,' marked by mutual penetration of past and present and succession without externality, as opposed to homogeneous, spatialized mathematical time.

beginner_explanation: The Stoic belief that the universe periodically burns up entirely and then starts over again, repeating the exact same history forever.
academic_explanation: The Stoic doctrine that the cosmos, which originated from pure fire, will periodically be reabsorbed into fire, after which an identical cosmic cycle recurs, eternally and without variation.

beginner_explanation: Bergson's name for the single creative life-force that pushes evolution forward, struggling against the resistance of matter.
academic_explanation: The 'vital impulse,' given once for all at the world's beginning, which Bergson takes to be the driving, creative force of biological evolution, opposed to and partly channeled by inert matter.

beginner_explanation: Rousseau's term for what we today call representative democracy (electing representatives), which he distinguishes from 'true' (direct) democracy.
academic_explanation: Rousseau's classification of representative government as 'elective aristocracy' rather than democracy proper, since he reserves the term 'democracy' for direct participation of every citizen, as in the ancient City State.

beginner_explanation: The idea that lower levels of reality flow or radiate outward from a higher, more perfect source, the way light radiates from the sun, without the source itself being diminished.
academic_explanation: The characteristic Neoplatonic model by which nous proceeds from the One, and Soul from nous, and the visible cosmos from Soul, each successive level a necessary but progressively less perfect 'outgoing' expression of the level above it, rather than a deliberate act of creation from nothing.
related_concepts: The visible world as beautiful, not evil

beginner_explanation: In Locke's day, this meant claiming to have a personal, direct revelation from God -- not excitement as we use the word today.
academic_explanation: Locke's term, discussed in his chapter 'Of Enthusiasm,' for unwarranted claims of personal revelation, which he regards as undermining rational, social truth-seeking and as flattering 'men's laziness, ignorance, and vanity.'

beginner_explanation: The original meaning of 'enthusiasm': having the god enter into you and feeling yourself become one with the god during ecstatic Dionysiac ritual.
academic_explanation: The state of ritual possession sought in Dionysiac (and, in refined form, Orphic) worship, in which the worshipper's ordinary consciousness is displaced by identification with the god; etymologically 'en-theos', having the god within.

beginner_explanation: Five Spartan officials chosen yearly who checked the power of the kings.
academic_explanation: A board of five annually selected magistrates, chosen by a method Aristotle called 'too childish' (effectively by lot), who held supreme civil jurisdiction and criminal authority even over the kings.

beginner_explanation: The view that the soul is made of physical particles (like fine breath or heat) spread through the body, and simply disperses -- ending all feeling -- when the body dies.
academic_explanation: Epicurus's doctrine that the soul consists of material atoms distributed through the body, responsible for sensation only while connected to a living body, and dispersing (with consequent loss of sensation, but not of the constituent atoms) at death.

beginner_explanation: A circle whose center moves along the edge of another circle, used by ancient astronomers to model the complicated apparent paths of the planets while keeping the earth at the center.
academic_explanation: A geometrical device, invented by Apollonius and developed by Hipparchus and Ptolemy, in which a planet moves on a small circle (epicycle) whose center in turn moves on a larger circle (deferent) around the earth, used to preserve geocentrism while matching observed planetary motion.
related_concepts: Hipparchus and the epicycle theory (toward the Ptolemaic system)

beginner_explanation: The idea that people should be treated unequally in proportion to their merit, rather than given strictly equal shares.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's proposed remedy for revolution, distributing political goods in proportion to virtue rather than by strict equality; Russell argues this collapses in practice into distribution by wealth, since virtue is not reliably measurable.
related_concepts: Causes of revolution and 'equality according to proportion'

beginner_explanation: The view that the state, not the Church, should have final authority over religious matters within a country.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, embraced by Hobbes in Part III of Leviathan, that the Church must be subordinate to the civil sovereign in each nation, denying any legitimate universal Church independent of national governments and rejecting papal overlordship and infallibility.
related_concepts: Absolute sovereignty and the rejection of divided or limited government

beginner_explanation: The practice of living alone as a religious hermit, withdrawn from society, in pursuit of holiness.
academic_explanation: The solitary ascetic form of early Christian monasticism, pioneered by Saint Anthony in Egypt from about 270 and carried to further extremes in Syria (e.g., Saint Simeon Stylites).

beginner_explanation: Latin for 'to be is to be perceived' -- Berkeley's slogan for the idea that things only exist while some mind is perceiving them.
academic_explanation: Berkeley's core idealist principle that the being (esse) of sensible objects consists entirely in their being perceived (percipi).

beginner_explanation: The properties something cannot lose without ceasing to be itself.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's term for what a thing is 'by its very nature' -- those properties definitional of it and of its species; Russell calls the notion 'muddle-headed' and 'incapable of precision.'

beginner_explanation: For Aristotle, not just a feeling of pleasure but living and acting well -- exercising your best abilities over the course of a whole life.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's term for the highest human good, defined as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life, with contemplative activity as its most perfect form.

beginner_explanation: The hidden assumption, in a statement like 'all Greeks are men,' that Greeks actually exist.
academic_explanation: The implicit claim that the subject class of a universal statement is non-empty, which Russell argues Aristotle's logic never separates from the purely hypothetical content of universal statements, producing formally invalid inferences when the subject class is empty (e.g., 'all golden mountains').
related_concepts: Formal defects: existential import and the particular/universal confusion

beginner_explanation: Latin for 'breath of the voice'; Roscelin's supposed description of universals as mere vocal sounds with no further reality.
academic_explanation: The phrase Anselm attributes to Roscelin to characterize his nominalist claim that a universal is nothing more than the physical event of uttering a word.

beginner_explanation: A center of Platonic study in Florence, founded and supported by the ruling Medici family.
academic_explanation: An institution founded by Cosimo dei Medici and continued by Lorenzo the Magnificent, devoted to the study of Plato, and central to the Renaissance revival of Platonism in competition with scholastic Aristotelianism.
related_concepts: The revival of Plato and genuine, first-hand classical scholarship

beginner_explanation: The idea that everything is constantly changing and nothing stays exactly the same from moment to moment.
academic_explanation: Heraclitus's doctrine, reported by Plato and Aristotle, that 'nothing ever is, everything is becoming' -- all things are in continuous process rather than possessing fixed being.

beginner_explanation: Rousseau's paradoxical claim that making someone obey the general will, even against their own wishes, is actually making them free.
academic_explanation: Rousseau's doctrine that whoever refuses to obey the general will 'shall be forced to do so,' which 'means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free' -- criticized by Russell as sophistical and later adopted, in modified form, by Hegel.

beginner_explanation: A paradoxical phrase associated with romantic-era political thought suggesting that compelling someone to obey a collective will is really making them free.
academic_explanation: Though fully developed in the Rousseau chapter, the concept has roots in the romantic elevation of a collective Ego (e.g. the nation) whose will can override the individual's while still being described as freedom.

beginner_explanation: The 'real' common interest of a community, different from just adding up what everyone individually wants, and always aimed at the public good.
academic_explanation: The will belonging to the body politic as such, distinct from the will of the majority and from the 'will of all' (sum of individual wills); always tends to the public advantage, though Rousseau does not clearly specify how it is empirically identified.

beginner_explanation: A rival religious-philosophical movement holding that the physical world and its creator are evil, and that only the human soul possesses genuine divinity.
academic_explanation: A family of late-antique religious-philosophical doctrines, addressed and rejected by Plotinus, holding that the material cosmos is the flawed or malevolent product of an inferior or evil creative power, and that salvation consists in the soul's escape from matter through esoteric knowledge (gnosis).
related_concepts: The visible world as beautiful, not evil

beginner_explanation: The idea that every virtue is a balanced middle point between two bad extremes -- for example, courage is the balance between cowardice and recklessness.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's doctrine that moral virtue is a disposition intermediate between two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency, relative to the agent and situation.

beginner_explanation: A roughly forty-year period (1378-1417) when there were two, and briefly three, rival popes, each recognized by different European states.
academic_explanation: The papal schism beginning with the disputed 1378 election of Urban VI (Rome) against Clement VII (Avignon), dividing Catholic Christendom along largely national political lines until resolved by the Council of Constance's election of Martin V in 1417.

beginner_explanation: The reasons we have for believing something is likely true, even without certainty -- mainly, either our own experience or the reliable testimony of others.
academic_explanation: Locke's term for the basis of 'degrees of assent': conformity with our own experience, or the testimony of others' experience.

beginner_explanation: The small ruling class in Plato's ideal city, chosen and trained to govern wisely.
academic_explanation: The politically empowered class in Plato's Republic, selected initially by the legislator and mainly hereditary thereafter, subject to exceptional promotion or demotion, who alone exercise political authority and undergo the most demanding education.

beginner_explanation: The names of the two rival factions in medieval Italian politics: Guelfs supported the Pope, Ghibellines supported the Emperor.
academic_explanation: Corruptions of 'Welf' and 'Waiblingen,' the family names of rival claimants to the imperial throne at the time of Frederick's contest with Emperor Otto; the terms subsequently named the pro-papal (Guelf) and pro-imperial (Ghibelline) factions across Italian city politics.

beginner_explanation: Russell's label (half-joking) for one branch of post-Kantian liberal thought that, he schematically suggests, led eventually toward Stalin.
academic_explanation: Russell's schematic characterization of the liberal line running through Bentham, Ricardo, and Marx.

beginner_explanation: The idea that things that seem opposed to each other, like the pull of a bowstring against the bow, actually work together to create something unified and functional.
academic_explanation: Heraclitus's doctrine that unity ('the one') is constituted by tension between opposites ('the many'), illustrated by the image of the strung bow or lyre, and later echoed in Hegelian dialectic.

beginner_explanation: Simmias's Pythagorean-inspired suggestion that the soul might just be like the 'tune' produced by the body, which can't outlive the instrument.
academic_explanation: The objection, raised by Simmias, that the soul is analogous to the harmony (attunement) produced by a lyre's strings, and so cannot survive the destruction of the body that produces it; rejected by Socrates on the grounds that a harmony is complex while the soul is simple.
related_concepts: The argument from the soul's simplicity

beginner_explanation: A pious, traditionalist Jewish party that resisted Greek cultural influence and Antiochus IV's persecution.
academic_explanation: A party of strict religious observance ('the Holy') strong among the rural population of Judea in the 2nd century B.C., forerunners, per Russell, of both the Pharisees and possibly the Essenes.

beginner_explanation: The view that pleasure is the only truly good thing, and pain the only truly bad thing.
academic_explanation: The ethical doctrine, foundational to Epicureanism, that pleasure is the beginning and end of the good life, with all other apparent goods (virtue, wisdom, justice) valued only instrumentally, as means to securing pleasure or avoiding pain.

beginner_explanation: What Hegel calls 'freedom' turns out to mean, in practice, little more than the right to obey the law of one's State -- not democracy, a free press, or individual liberty in the ordinary liberal sense.
academic_explanation: Hegel's technical redefinition of freedom as self-determination through law -- 'there is no freedom without law,' converted (per Russell) into the claim that wherever there is law there is freedom, such that even a monarch's imprisonment of a liberal subject counts as Spirit 'freely determining itself.'

beginner_explanation: Mahomet's flight from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD, which marks the start of the Islamic calendar.
academic_explanation: The emigration (hijra) of Muhammad and his followers from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE, adopted as year one of the Islamic (Hijri) calendar.

beginner_explanation: The theory that the sun, not the earth, is at the center of the solar system, with the earth and planets orbiting it.
academic_explanation: The astronomical hypothesis, advanced by Aristarchus of Samos and later adopted as definite by Seleucus, that the sun remains fixed while the earth and other planets revolve around it in circular orbits, with the earth additionally rotating daily on its own axis.

beginner_explanation: The idea that the sun, not the earth, is at the center of the solar system, with the earth both spinning on its axis and orbiting the sun.
academic_explanation: The astronomical model, proposed cautiously by Copernicus and confirmed and refined by Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, in which the sun occupies (approximately) the center of the planetary system and the earth undergoes both diurnal rotation and annual revolution, displacing the geocentric Ptolemaic model.
related_concepts: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion

beginner_explanation: The period and culture of the Greek-speaking world after Alexander the Great's conquests, roughly 323 to 30 B.C., when Greek civilization spread across the Middle East and mixed heavily with local cultures.
academic_explanation: The era following the death of Alexander the Great, characterized by the Macedonian successor kingdoms (Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Antigonid), a diffusion and internal transformation of Greek language and culture across a vastly enlarged geographic area, and the foundation of the Epicurean, Stoic, and formal Sceptical schools of philosophy.

beginner_explanation: The enslaved native population of Laconia and Messenia who farmed the land for their Spartan masters.
academic_explanation: A hereditary serf class bound to Spartan land-lots, required to render fixed produce quotas to their landowners, and subject to periodic state-sanctioned killing to suppress rebellion.

beginner_explanation: The view, shared by Hegel and (per Russell, citing Jan Smuts) other philosophers, that things can only be truly understood in terms of their relations to the whole they belong to, not in isolation.
academic_explanation: The metaphysical (and, separately, ethical) thesis that reality (or value) belongs primarily or exclusively to wholes rather than to their parts taken separately; Russell attributes an implicit holism to Hegel's system and subjects it to sustained logical criticism.

beginner_explanation: The revived Western Roman Empire, founded when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor on Christmas Day, 800, which lasted (in one form or another) until Napoleon's time.
academic_explanation: The medieval and early-modern political entity founded by Charlemagne's imperial coronation, whose constitution assumed a theoretical harmony between Pope and Emperor, and whose relationship to the papacy was one of structural interdependence and recurring conflict.
related_concepts: The mutual dependence of Pope and Emperor

beginner_explanation: The two characters in Berkeley's dialogue: Hylas defends ordinary belief in matter, Philonous (Berkeley's own view) argues him out of it.
academic_explanation: The two interlocutors of Berkeley's Dialogues Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, representing respectively scientifically educated common sense (Hylas) and Berkeley's immaterialist idealism (Philonous).

beginner_explanation: A fainter, copied version of an impression -- like remembering or imagining red, rather than actually seeing it.
academic_explanation: Hume's term for the 'faint images' of impressions occurring in thinking, reasoning, memory, and imagination; simple ideas must resemble a corresponding simple impression.

beginner_explanation: In Plato's theory, the single, perfect, eternal version of something (like 'the bed' or 'beauty itself'), of which all the ordinary examples we see are only imperfect copies.
academic_explanation: The timeless, non-spatial universal that Plato holds is the true referent of a general term, in which many particular things imperfectly 'participate,' and which alone can be an object of knowledge as opposed to opinion.

beginner_explanation: Bacon's name for common bad mental habits that lead people into error -- biases built into human nature, personal prejudice, being misled by imprecise words, blind deference to received authorities like Aristotle, and letting rigid rules replace real judgment.
academic_explanation: Bacon's fivefold classification of sources of intellectual error: idols of the tribe (biases inherent in human nature), idols of the cave (an individual investigator's personal prejudices), idols of the market-place (errors arising from the imprecision and tyranny of language), idols of the theatre (uncritical acceptance of received systems of thought, chiefly Aristotelian and scholastic), and idols of the schools (substituting a blind rule, such as the syllogism, for genuine judgement).
related_concepts: The doctrine of the 'idols' (bad habits of mind)

beginner_explanation: Bergson's word for the basic 'stuff' of the universe -- something midway between a mental representation and a real external thing, meant to avoid choosing between idealism and realism.
academic_explanation: Bergson's neutral term, defined in Matter and Memory as 'an existence... more than... a representation, but less than... a thing,' which Russell argues in practice smuggles in an unresolved confusion between the mental act of imaging and the object imaged.

beginner_explanation: An Athenian law that made it a crime not to practice the state religion or to teach unconventional theories about the heavens.
academic_explanation: A law permitting the impeachment of those who did not practise religion or who taught theories about 'the things on high,' used to prosecute Anaxagoras for his naturalistic claims about the sun and moon, and later revived against Socrates.

beginner_explanation: A vivid, direct experience -- like actually seeing red or feeling pain -- as opposed to just imagining or remembering it.
academic_explanation: Hume's term for perceptions with 'more force and violence,' the original, direct data of sensation and feeling from which all simple ideas are copied.

beginner_explanation: Two lengths (like the side and diagonal of a square) that cannot both be measured exactly by whole-number multiples of some common unit.
academic_explanation: Magnitudes between which there exists no ratio of integers m:n such that m times one equals n times the other; discovered via the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit right isosceles triangle, and later handled rigorously in Euclid, Book X.

beginner_explanation: The idea that the individual person, not the group, is the basic unit whose judgment, rights, or value matter most.
academic_explanation: Russell's umbrella term covering intellectual individualism (private judgment as the arbiter of truth), economic individualism (property and free enterprise), and emotional/ethical individualism (self-assertion and heroism), each with distinct historical origins and political consequences.

beginner_explanation: Concluding a general rule just because every example checked so far fits it -- which can go wrong, as illustrated by Bacon's parable of a census-taker who wrongly assumes every villager shares one name after meeting many people in a row who do.
academic_explanation: A form of inductive inference that generalizes from an unbroken run of confirming instances without any further justification for the generalization; Bacon sought a superior inductive method to replace it for detailed scientific investigation, though Russell notes it remains, even in comprehensive scientific laws, an ultimately unavoidable foundation.
related_concepts: Induction by simple enumeration and its unreliability

beginner_explanation: Payments or acts of devotion the medieval Catholic Church said could reduce the punishment owed for sin -- a major source of papal revenue that the Reformers rejected as false.
academic_explanation: A remission, granted by the Church, of temporal punishment due for sins already forgiven, historically obtainable in part through payment; rejection of Indulgences by Luther and Calvin removed a large source of papal revenue and was central to the early Reformation controversy.
related_concepts: Predestination versus free will and works
The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology

beginner_explanation: The active process of turning a confusing, unsettled situation into a clear, organized one.
academic_explanation: Defined by Dewey as 'the controlled or directed transformation of an indeterminate situation into one that is so determinate in its constituent distinctions and relations as to convert the elements of the original situation into a unified whole.'

beginner_explanation: A Church institution founded to investigate and prosecute heresy, using harsh methods including torture and execution.
academic_explanation: A judicial institution founded by Gregory IX in 1233, primarily staffed by Dominicans and Franciscans, to systematize the prosecution of heresy (and later sorcery and witchcraft) previously handled less formally by bishops; denied the accused counsel after 1254 and handed convicted heretics to secular authorities for execution.

beginner_explanation: Dewey's version of pragmatism, which treats beliefs and theories as tools for successfully handling situations rather than as fixed pictures of an unchanging truth.
academic_explanation: Dewey's doctrine substituting 'inquiry' -- the controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate, unified one -- for 'truth' as logic's fundamental concept.

beginner_explanation: For Bergson, a refined, self-aware form of instinct that can grasp the living flow of reality directly, unlike the analytic, spatializing intellect.
academic_explanation: Bergson's term for 'instinct that has become disinterested, self-conscious, capable of reflecting upon its object and of enlarging it indefinitely,' contrasted with intellect's spatial, analytic mode of cognition.

beginner_explanation: The ceremony in which a new bishop received the symbols (ring and staff) of his office; the dispute was over whether the king/emperor or the Pope had the right to grant them.
academic_explanation: The ceremonial conferral of the ring and staff symbolizing episcopal office, historically performed by the bishop's feudal overlord; Gregory VII's insistence that only the Pope could invest bishops triggered the Investiture Controversy with Henry IV.
related_concepts: The Investiture Controversy and the conflict of Gregory VII and Henry IV

beginner_explanation: What you get once you put a raw sensation into words or connect it with memory -- for example, judging 'this shade of red is like that one.'
academic_explanation: Russell's term for a percept 'filled out' with words and memories, and thereby rendered capable of truth or falsehood; he argues the thesis 'knowledge is perception' is defensible only if reinterpreted as 'knowledge is judgements of perception.'

beginner_explanation: Natural law (rules that apply to all people everywhere by virtue of reason) versus the actual laws and customs of particular nations.
academic_explanation: A Stoic legal-philosophical distinction between jus naturale, a universal law derivable from self-evident rational first principles common to all mankind, and jus gentium, the variable positive law and custom of individual peoples.
related_concepts: Natural law and natural human equality

beginner_explanation: Plato's final answer to 'what is justice?': everyone sticking to their own role and not meddling in others'.
academic_explanation: Plato's Republic Book IV definition of justice as each class or individual performing its proper function without interference in others', tracing back to an older Greek notion of cosmic order and appointed place.

beginner_explanation: The idea that fairness means giving each person what fits their own worth or merit, not necessarily the same as everyone else.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's view that justice consists in proportionate rather than strictly equal distribution, applied to relationships of unequal worth such as master/slave, parent/child, husband/wife.

beginner_explanation: The idea that something's economic value comes mainly from the work put into making or improving it, not from the raw material alone.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, traced by Russell from Aquinas through Locke to Ricardo and Marx, that the value of a product is (largely) determined by the labour expended in producing it.

beginner_explanation: The principle that a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at a constant speed forever unless something acts on it to change its speed or direction.
academic_explanation: Galileo's discovery, formalized by Newton as the first law of motion, that uniform rectilinear motion, not rest or circular motion, is the 'natural' state of a body absent external force; acceleration (change of velocity in magnitude or direction) thereby becomes the central explanatory concept of dynamics.
related_concepts: The law of inertia and the abandonment of 'natural' places and motions

beginner_explanation: For Locke, a set of moral rules given by God (like 'don't harm others') that apply even without any human government to enforce them.
academic_explanation: Locke's term for divinely grounded moral obligations binding all rational persons in the state of nature, independent of positive (human-made) law.

beginner_explanation: Hobbes's name for the state itself, imagined as a giant artificial person made up of all its citizens, with the sovereign acting as its 'soul.'
academic_explanation: Hobbes's figure for the Commonwealth as an artificial man created by the covenant among citizens, with sovereignty functioning as its 'artificial soul,' and the pacts creating it likened to God's creative fiat.
related_concepts: The social contract and the creation of 'Leviathan'

beginner_explanation: The first wave of political thought favoring religious tolerance, free commerce, and government based on the people's consent rather than a king's supposed divine right.
academic_explanation: A seventeenth-to-eighteenth-century English and Dutch political-philosophical outlook combining latitudinarian Protestantism, respect for property and commerce, restriction of hereditary privilege, and government legitimated by consent, later given systematic philosophical form by Locke.

beginner_explanation: Something that seems, from ordinary language, to be a 'thing' (like the number two) but which, once the sentence using it is properly analysed, turns out not to correspond to any single object at all.
academic_explanation: Russell's term for entities such as numbers, which are not constituents of the facts that verify statements about them but only common logical forms; e.g. 'I have two hands' contains, on analysis, no constituent corresponding to the word 'two.'

beginner_explanation: The idea that all of mathematics can ultimately be built out of pure logic, so that mathematical truths are really just truths about what our terms mean.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, developed by Frege and worked out in detail by Whitehead and Russell in Principia Mathematica, that arithmetic and pure mathematics are 'nothing but a prolongation of deductive logic,' making mathematical knowledge 'merely verbal' rather than empirical or synthetic a priori.

beginner_explanation: A Greek philosophical term for divine reason or 'the Word,' which the Gospel of John uses to describe Christ.
academic_explanation: The Platonic-Stoic concept of a rational divine ordering principle, identified in the Fourth Gospel with Christ ('In the beginning was the Word'), marking the point where Jewish-Christian simplicity gives way to Greek theological vocabulary.

beginner_explanation: The rational principle the Stoics believed runs through and governs the entire universe, identified with God, Nature, and Destiny all at once.
academic_explanation: In Stoic metaphysics, the active, rational, providential principle (also called God, Zeus, Nature, or Destiny) that structures and directs the material cosmos according to fixed law, and a 'spark' of which is present in every human being's rational soul.

beginner_explanation: English followers of John Wycliffe who were persecuted and largely suppressed.
academic_explanation: The English religious movement following Wycliffe's teachings, severely persecuted and practically stamped out after his death, though the underlying anti-papal sentiment survived underground and helped prepare English ground for later Protestantism.

beginner_explanation: An alliance of independent Northern Italian cities, led by Milan, that resisted the Holy Roman Emperor and allied with the Pope.
academic_explanation: A military and political league of North Italian communes formed to resist Emperor Frederick Barbarossa's assertions of overlordship, defeating him decisively at Legnano in 1176.

beginner_explanation: Two opposing cosmic forces Empedocles believed drive all change: Love brings the elements together, and Strife pulls them apart.
academic_explanation: Two primitive forces, treated as substances on a level with the four elements, whose alternating dominance in a repeating cosmic cycle explains the combination and separation of the elements, and hence all coming-to-be and passing-away.

beginner_explanation: The legendary lawgiver credited with creating Sparta's constitution and way of life.
academic_explanation: A probably mythical (originally divine) figure to whom later tradition, especially Plutarch, attributed the entirety of the Spartan constitution and social system, though Russell notes the system in fact grew up gradually.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's picture of the ideally proud man -- dignified, self-sufficient, only moderately pleased by honours, and contemptuous of trivial concerns.
academic_explanation: The virtue Aristotle treats as the 'crown' of the other virtues, presupposing exceptional social position and worth, and concerned chiefly with the proper attitude toward honour and dishonour.

term: Man is the measure of all things
beginner_explanation: Protagoras's famous saying meaning that truth depends on each individual person's own perception or judgment, with no independent standard to say who is right.
academic_explanation: Protagoras's relativist thesis, interpreted by Russell as holding that when individuals' judgments conflict, there is no objective truth by which one can be shown correct and the other incorrect, grounded in scepticism about the reliability of sense-perception.
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

beginner_explanation: A religion mixing Christian and Persian (Zoroastrian) ideas, teaching that evil is a real, physical force and that all sex and meat-eating are wrong.
academic_explanation: A dualist religion founded by Mani, combining Christian and Zoroastrian elements, holding evil to be a positive principle embodied in matter and good embodied in spirit; notable in this chapter as the sect through which Saint Augustine passed before his conversion to Catholicism.

beginner_explanation: The idea that a society's ideas, religion, art, and politics are largely shaped by how it produces and distributes goods.
academic_explanation: Marx's doctrine that the politics, religion, philosophy, and art of an epoch are, in broad outline, an outcome of its methods of production and distribution, replacing Hegel's Spirit-driven history with an economically driven one.

beginner_explanation: Matter is what a thing is made of; form is the shape or structure that makes that material into a definite, particular thing.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's hylomorphic distinction: matter is potentiality, form is the actualizing principle that confers definiteness and, in Aristotle's view, greater reality and substantiality on a compound.
related_concepts: Soul as form of the body

beginner_explanation: Explaining an event by what caused it beforehand, rather than by what purpose it serves.
academic_explanation: An explanation that answers the question 'what earlier circumstances caused this event,' as opposed to a teleological explanation, which answers 'what purpose did this event serve'; the method Russell credits the atomists with pioneering.

beginner_explanation: Religious orders, like the Franciscans and Dominicans, whose members took vows of poverty and lived by begging rather than owning property.
academic_explanation: Thirteenth-century religious orders (chiefly Franciscan and Dominican) founded on a rule of corporate and individual poverty, sustained by alms rather than fixed endowments; they came to dominate both popular preaching and, in the Dominican case especially, university scholarship.
related_concepts: Saint Francis, the Franciscan order, and its ironic institutional fate

beginner_explanation: A technique for finding the area of a curved shape (like a circle) by fitting many-sided polygons inside and outside it, getting closer and closer to the true area.
academic_explanation: A rigorous technique, developed by Eudoxus and used extensively by Archimedes, for establishing the measure of a curved figure via polygonal approximations that can be made to differ from the true value by less than any assigned quantity, anticipating the integral calculus.
related_concepts: The method of exhaustion (an anticipation of the calculus)

beginner_explanation: The advanced, art-loving seafaring civilization of ancient Crete, roughly 2500 to 1400 B.C., discovered mainly through the excavations of Sir Arthur Evans.
academic_explanation: A Bronze Age maritime civilization centered on Crete, characterized by unwalled, sea-defended cities, close commercial contact with Egypt, and a still-undeciphered linear script, which spread to the Greek mainland as the Mycenaean civilization before its own destruction around the end of the fourteenth century B.C.

beginner_explanation: A Persian-origin religion centered on the god Mithras, popular especially among Roman soldiers, and a serious rival to early Christianity for a time.
academic_explanation: A mystery religion of Persian origin, centered on the warrior sun-god Mithras and a cosmic struggle between good and evil derived from Zoroastrian tradition, which spread widely among the Roman army in the third century A.D. and competed directly with Christianity before the latter's establishment as the state religion.
related_concepts: The spread of Eastern religion and superstition in the Western Empire

beginner_explanation: A particular way in which the one substance shows up - like a wave is a particular shape water takes.
academic_explanation: A finite, dependent modification or aspect of the single infinite substance; individual minds and bodies are modes, not substances, for Spinoza.

beginner_explanation: One of the countless simple, soul-like units Leibniz believed everything in the universe is really made of.
academic_explanation: A simple, unextended substance that perceives the universe from its own point of view with varying clarity; monads are 'windowless' and do not causally interact.

beginner_explanation: The teaching, also condemned as heretical, that Christ had only one nature rather than two (human and divine) joined in one person.
academic_explanation: The doctrine that Christ possesses a single nature, condemned at the Council of Chalcedon (451) in favor of the formula of two natures united in one Person; adopted widely in Egypt and Abyssinia.

beginner_explanation: Plato's poetic name for time: a created, ever-changing copy of changeless eternity.
academic_explanation: Timaeus's characterization of time as a created entity, proceeding 'according to number,' that imitates the changeless unity of eternity as closely as something in motion can.
related_concepts: Time as 'the moving image of eternity'

beginner_explanation: Hume's term for the fact that, whatever philosophy proves or fails to prove, human nature simply forces us to go on believing in cause and effect, an external world, and so on.
academic_explanation: Hume's appeal, in the face of his own total scepticism, to an unavoidable, non-rational psychological disposition ('nature ... has determined us to judge') that sustains ordinary belief despite the absence of rational justification.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's claim that some people are naturally suited only to be ruled by others and can rightly be enslaved.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's doctrine that certain individuals, naturally deficient in reason, are fit only for subjection, making their enslavement expedient and just, extended (controversially) to justify war against peoples deemed naturally fit to be ruled.

beginner_explanation: The teaching, condemned as heretical, that Christ was two separate persons -- one human, one divine -- rather than a single unified person.
academic_explanation: The Christological position associated with Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, condemned at the Council of Ephesus (431), which spread as a distinct church across Syria, Persia, India, and eventually China.

beginner_explanation: The idea that the basic 'stuff' of the universe is neither mental nor physical, but something more basic that can show up as either.
academic_explanation: A doctrine developed by James's followers (not James himself) as an implication of radical empiricism: reality is composed of a single kind of neutral material, anterior to the mind/matter distinction.

beginner_explanation: The official Christian statement of belief, produced to settle the dispute over whether Jesus is fully equal to God the Father.
academic_explanation: The doctrinal statement produced (in preliminary form) at the Council of Nicaea (325) affirming the equality and identity of substance of the Father and the Son as distinct Persons, becoming the touchstone of orthodoxy against both Arianism and Sabellianism.

beginner_explanation: A Buddhist term for liberation from suffering, which Schopenhauer interprets specifically as extinction -- the ending of individual will and, ultimately, of the phenomenal world as such.
academic_explanation: The goal of Schopenhauer's ascetic path, interpreted as the extinction of will and, with it, of the entire objectified phenomenal world; Russell notes Schopenhauer's own text leaves this goal 'wholly and entirely negative,' with no positive content comparable to Christian mystical union with God.

beginner_explanation: An approach to ethics that looks down on ordinary pleasure and happiness as unworthy goals, favoring things like heroism or duty instead.
academic_explanation: Russell's term for ethical systems (e.g., Kant's) that reject pleasure/happiness as the good in favor of ostensibly higher ends such as duty or heroic self-sacrifice.

beginner_explanation: A myth the government deliberately teaches, saying people are born of gold, silver, or bronze/iron, to justify the class system.
academic_explanation: The 'one royal lie' Plato proposes the state inculcate, holding that God made guardians of gold, soldiers of silver, and producers of bronze and iron, intended to secure across-generation acceptance of the class hierarchy.

beginner_explanation: The 'nominal essence' of a thing is just how we define the word for it; the 'real essence' is its actual, often unknown, physical makeup.
academic_explanation: Locke's distinction, in Book III of the Essay, between the verbal definition attached to a general term (nominal essence) and a thing's unknown underlying physical constitution (real essence), used to dissolve the scholastic doctrine of essence.

beginner_explanation: The view that general terms like 'cat' or 'man' are just names or words, without any independently existing reality corresponding to them.
academic_explanation: The philosophical position, associated in this chapter with Roscelin, that universals have no reality beyond individual particulars and the words used to group them; contrasted with realism.

beginner_explanation: Reasoning that gives you a probable, but not logically certain, conclusion -- like inferring that other people have feelings, or that the sun will rise tomorrow.
academic_explanation: Inference that is not strictly deductive (i.e., not logically guaranteed by its premises), including inductive and analogical inference, central to the question of what we can validly infer beyond our own immediate percepts.

beginner_explanation: Bentham's dismissive phrase for the idea of natural, inborn human rights, which he thought was empty and meaningless.
academic_explanation: Bentham's characterization of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man's claim to 'imprescriptible rights,' which he classified as either unintelligible, false, or both.

beginner_explanation: The Greek philosophical term for 'intellect' or the rational, thinking part of the mind, as distinct from the individual soul.
academic_explanation: In Aristotelian psychology, the faculty of intellectual understanding; Averroes held nous to be one and impersonal across all thinkers, and therefore immortal, in contrast to the individual, non-immortal soul.

beginner_explanation: Anaxagoras's name for a special, pure kind of 'stuff' that causes motion and makes living things different from non-living matter.
academic_explanation: In Anaxagoras's system, a substance distinct from and unmixed with all other matter, infinite and self-ruled, that enters into the composition of living things and originates the cosmic rotation that produces motion and the separation of light and heavy matter.

beginner_explanation: The 'second person' of Plotinus's divine hierarchy: a kind of divine Mind that contemplates the One and, in doing so, contains all the eternal Forms or ideas.
academic_explanation: The second hypostasis in Plotinus's system, engendered as the 'image' of the One through the One's self-directed vision; nous contains the eternal Forms/ideas and represents the highest form of intellectual activity, standing between the wholly transcendent One and the created Soul.

beginner_explanation: The principle that you shouldn't assume more things exist than you need to explain the facts.
academic_explanation: A methodological principle associated with William of Occam (though not found verbatim in his works) holding that explanations should posit the fewest possible entities; closest to his own phrasing, 'It is vain to do with more what can be done with fewer.'
related_concepts: Terms of first and second intention

beginner_explanation: The idea, proposed by Descartes's follower Geulincx, that mind and body don't actually cause each other to act -- they're more like two clocks wound up by God to keep perfect time, so it only looks like one causes the other.
