academic_explanation: Arnold Geulincx's theory that mind and body, being radically dissimilar substances incapable of true causal interaction, are instead kept in perfect correspondence by God, such that bodily events accompanying mental ones (and vice versa) are merely parallel, not causally connected -- a response to the physical impossibility (given the conservation of momentum) of Descartes's own pineal-gland mechanism.
related_concepts: Mind-body dualism and the pineal gland

beginner_explanation: John the Scot's major philosophical work, dividing everything that exists (and does not exist) into four classes, with God appearing as both the beginning and the end of all things.
academic_explanation: John the Scot's systematic Neoplatonic-Christian metaphysical treatise (De Divisione Naturae), organizing all being into a fourfold scheme of creating/created relations, culminating in a doctrine of universal return to God; repeatedly condemned as heretical and ordered burned by Pope Honorius III in 1225.
related_concepts: The Division of Nature (the fourfold classification of being)

beginner_explanation: An argument that tries to prove God exists just by carefully thinking about what 'God' means, without needing any evidence from the world.
academic_explanation: Saint Anselm's a priori argument that God, defined as the greatest possible object of thought, must exist, since a merely conceived but non-existent being would be surpassed in greatness by an otherwise identical being that does exist.

beginner_explanation: The claim that God's existence can be proven just from understanding the concept of God, without needing any other evidence.
academic_explanation: The a priori argument (associated with Anselm) that God's existence follows from His definition as the being than which none greater can be conceived; Aquinas rejects it on the grounds that human beings do not know God's essence with sufficient completeness to perform this deduction.

beginner_explanation: A mystical reform of the worship of Dionysus that taught the soul could be reborn many times and could ultimately be purified and freed from an endless cycle of birth and death.
academic_explanation: A Greek religious movement, traditionally traced to the figure of Orpheus, that organized itself into voluntary communities open to initiates regardless of race or sex, taught the transmigration of souls and their potential ascent to divine status through ritual and ascetic purification, and substantially shaped the religious dimension of Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy.

beginner_explanation: The belief that God and the universe are really the same thing, so that everything that exists is part of God.
academic_explanation: The view, developed most fully by Spinoza and attractive to many mystics, that denies a real distinction between God and the created world; contrasted by Russell with Augustine's orthodox insistence on creation ex nihilo.

beginner_explanation: Euclid's assumption about parallel lines, which he could not prove from his other axioms but stated openly rather than hiding.
academic_explanation: The fifth postulate of Euclid's Elements, whose independence from Euclid's other axioms was suspected for centuries and confirmed only by the development of non-Euclidean geometries in the nineteenth century.

beginner_explanation: An emotion you experience passively, as something happening to you from outside, rather than something you understand and control.
academic_explanation: An emotion arising from inadequate (confused) ideas; it ceases to be a passion once the mind forms a clear and distinct idea of it.

beginner_explanation: Sir Robert Filmer's book arguing that kings inherit their authority from Adam, the first father, making royal power a form of paternal power.
academic_explanation: Filmer's 1680 treatise grounding absolute monarchical authority in the patriarchal power God is said to have granted Adam over all his descendants.

beginner_explanation: The roughly two-century period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire, beginning with Augustus, that allowed trade, culture, and learning to spread safely across a huge territory.
academic_explanation: The extended period of internal peace and unified administration inaugurated by Augustus (30 B.C.) and lasting, with interruptions, until the crises of the third century A.D., during which Russell argues the Roman state functioned as the essential vehicle for diffusing and preserving Hellenistic civilization across a vastly enlarged territory.
related_concepts: The Roman peace as a preserving and diffusing force

beginner_explanation: The rival Christian teaching that people have full free will and can earn their way to heaven through their own good conduct, without needing unearned divine grace.
academic_explanation: The heresy taught by Pelagius, denying inherited original sin and affirming that virtuous action, freely chosen, is rewarded with salvation on its own merits; condemned largely through Augustine's efforts and finally at the Council of Orange (529).

beginner_explanation: A long war (431-404 B.C.) between Athens and Sparta that ended with Athens's total defeat.
academic_explanation: The conflict, arising from friction between Athenian imperial policy and Spartan interests, that Russell identifies as the external threat which, combined with internal democratic pressure, destroyed the Periclean balance of forces and ended Athenian political dominance.

beginner_explanation: A raw bit of sensory experience -- like a patch of colour or a sound -- before it has been interpreted or put into words.
academic_explanation: In Russell's usage, the bare occurrence given in sensation, belonging equally to the physical and the psychological orders, which is in itself neither true nor false and therefore cannot by itself constitute knowledge.

beginner_explanation: The roughly thirty-year period when the statesman Pericles led Athens and the city reached its cultural peak.
academic_explanation: The period of Athenian political and cultural pre-eminence under the elected leadership of Pericles, ending with his fall from power and death in 430/429 B.C., during which the Parthenon was built and Attic tragedy, comedy, sculpture, and historiography flourished.

beginner_explanation: Free people living in Spartan territory who had no political power.
academic_explanation: Free inhabitants of Laconia outside the Spartan citizen class, permitted personal liberty and property but excluded entirely from political power.

beginner_explanation: A Jewish religious group known for strict devotion to the Law, out of which some strands of early Christian ethics arguably grew.
academic_explanation: A Jewish religious-political party descended from the Hasidim, emphasizing strict adherence to the Law; Russell notes that, while later Christian tradition views Pharisees negatively, some Pharisaic ethical writing (e.g., the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs) closely anticipates the ethics of the Gospels.

beginner_explanation: A group of English thinkers led by Jeremy Bentham who wanted to reform law, government, and economics according to the single test of whether a policy produced 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number.'
academic_explanation: The English utilitarian reform movement led by Bentham, including James Mill, John Stuart Mill, and (loosely) Malthus, distinguished from French revolutionary rationalism by its patient attention to practical and economic detail and its rejection of the doctrine of natural rights.

beginner_explanation: The idea that many philosophical problems are really problems about the logical structure of language, which dissolve once that structure is made clear.
academic_explanation: Carnap's view, discussed and partly endorsed by Russell, that a great part of philosophy reduces to syntax in a wide sense, such that correcting syntactic errors solves or dissolves many traditional philosophical problems -- illustrated by, though not limited to, the theory of descriptions.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's word for 'nature,' closely tied to growth -- the 'nature' of an acorn is to grow into an oak.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's technical concept of a thing's end or telos, applied to whatever possesses an internal principle of motion, growth, or rest, distinguishing what exists 'by nature' from what exists through other, external causes.

beginner_explanation: A universe completely full of matter, with no empty space anywhere.
academic_explanation: A space entirely filled with being/matter, with no void; both Parmenides's monism and Descartes's later theory of extension imply a plenum, in which, it was widely assumed in antiquity, motion is impossible.
related_concepts: The void as a response to Parmenides

beginner_explanation: The idea that some people just know how to govern well, and that they should be the ones in charge.
academic_explanation: A generalized capacity for good governance, distinct from specialized craft-skills, that Plato holds consists in knowledge of the Good; Russell questions both its existence in this strong sense and, even if granted, the possibility of a constitution reliably selecting for it.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's term for the good version of rule by the many, aimed at the common good rather than narrow self-interest.
academic_explanation: The good, non-corrupted form of rule by the many in Aristotle's sixfold constitutional taxonomy, retaining, per Aristotle, some oligarchic elements and distinguished from democracy chiefly by aiming at the common good.

beginner_explanation: A modern nickname for the period in the tenth century when the Roman noblewoman Marozia and her family effectively controlled the selection of popes, including her own son and grandson.
academic_explanation: Russell's account of the tenth-century domination of the papacy by the Theophylact-Marozia family of Roman aristocrats, exemplified by Popes Sergius III, John XI (Marozia's son), and John XII (her grandson, elected at sixteen), whose 'debauched life' Russell quotes the Cambridge Medieval History as describing.
related_concepts: Russell's critique of 'the Dark Ages' as a Eurocentric label

beginner_explanation: A block of marble is only a 'potential' statue; once shaped, it becomes an 'actual' one. Change, for Aristotle, is the movement from potential to actual.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's dynamic complement to matter and form: matter is pure potentiality of form, actuality is the realized state; that which has more form is more actual, with God as pure actuality and no potentiality whatsoever.

beginner_explanation: A way of thinking, encouraged by science-as-technology, that cares only about whether something can be done efficiently, not about whether it should be done.
academic_explanation: Russell's term for philosophies inspired by scientific technique that 'tend to regard everything non-human as mere raw material,' valuing 'the skilfulness of the process' over the goodness of ends, which he identifies as the most dangerous intellectual tendency of his own era.
related_concepts: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'

beginner_explanation: Theoretical science tries to understand the world; practical science (technology) tries to change it.
academic_explanation: Russell's distinction between theoretical science, 'an attempt to understand the world,' and practical science, 'an attempt to change the world,' with the latter increasingly dominant from the sixteenth century onward and central to his account of the 'power philosophy.'
related_concepts: Science as technique and the 'power philosophy'

beginner_explanation: A modern philosophical movement that judges beliefs partly by their practical usefulness or consequences rather than by correspondence to an abstract, fixed truth alone.
academic_explanation: A twentieth-century philosophical school, represented here by F.C.S. Schiller, that Russell connects to Protagoras via the Theaetetus's suggestion that opinions can be evaluated as 'better' or 'worse' by their practical fitness even where they cannot be shown objectively 'truer.'
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

beginner_explanation: God's advance arrangement that makes all the separate, non-interacting monads appear to affect each other, like clocks set in advance to strike together.
academic_explanation: Leibniz's doctrine that apparent causal interaction between substances is really the result of each substance's independent, God-ordained unfolding matching every other's.

beginner_explanation: The idea that God has already decided, in advance and without regard to anyone's merit, who will be saved and who will be damned.
academic_explanation: Augustine's doctrine that God elects certain persons to salvation by grace alone, an unmotivated choice not grounded in the merits or demerits of the elect, developed chiefly against Pelagius.
related_concepts: Predestination versus free will and works

beginner_explanation: The idea that some properties of things (like weight or hardness) are really in the object, while others (like colour, taste, or warmth) only exist because of how our senses respond.
academic_explanation: Democritus's distinction between qualities 'of the understanding,' held to be genuinely in the object (weight, density, hardness), and qualities 'of the senses,' held to depend on the perceiver's sense-organs and therefore to be potentially deceptive (warmth, taste, colour); explicitly compared by Russell to Locke's later distinction.
related_concepts: Perception and the primary/secondary quality distinction

beginner_explanation: Properties like shape, solidity, and motion that Locke thought really belong to objects themselves.
academic_explanation: Qualities Locke defines as 'inseparable from body': solidity, extension, figure, motion or rest, and number.

beginner_explanation: The rule that the eldest child (usually eldest son) automatically inherits everything.
academic_explanation: An inheritance rule Locke criticizes as unjust, and as an unavoidable but arbitrary consequence of grounding legitimate authority on heredity.
related_concepts: Filmer's patriarchal theory of divine right

beginner_explanation: The question of what makes two individual things of the same kind actually two separate things rather than one.
academic_explanation: The scholastic problem of identifying the metaphysical ground of numerical distinctness among individuals of a shared species or essence; Duns Scotus locates it in form, Aquinas (for material things) in differentiated spatial position within matter.

beginner_explanation: Schopenhauer's scholastic term for space and time -- the features of experience that make things separate and countable as 'many' rather than 'one.'
academic_explanation: Schopenhauer's term, adapted from scholastic philosophy, for space and time as the source of plurality/individuation among phenomena; since (per Kant) space and time are merely phenomenal, the underlying Will cannot be individuated and must be single.

beginner_explanation: The idea that evil is not a real, positive thing in itself, but simply the absence or lack of good.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, held by John the Scot (with Neoplatonic and Augustinian roots), that evil has no independent ontological ground or ground of necessity, being instead a privation -- a not-being -- rather than a created substance.

beginner_explanation: The idea that evil is not a real 'thing' but simply the absence of good, the way darkness is the absence of light.
academic_explanation: Boethius's Platonic doctrine that evil has no positive existence but is a privation (deficiency) of good, deduced from God's omnipotence and perfect goodness.

beginner_explanation: The puzzle of what general words like 'dog' or 'red' actually refer to, since the world seems to contain only individual things.
academic_explanation: The question of the ontological status of general and relational terms, first sharply posed, per Russell, by the logical part of Plato's theory of Ideas, and unresolved 'to the present day.'

beginner_explanation: The unknown author of an influential Christian-Neoplatonist text, wrongly believed in the Middle Ages to be a convert of Saint Paul mentioned in Acts, whose work John the Scot translated into Latin.
academic_explanation: The pseudonymous author (probably a disciple of Proclus, writing after Plotinus and before A.D. 500) of works reconciling Neoplatonism with Christian theology, whose mistaken identification with Saint Paul's Athenian convert (Acts 17:34) gave his apophatic theology exceptional authority in medieval Catholic philosophy once John the Scot translated it into Latin in 860.
related_concepts: Negative (apophatic) theology and the unknowability of God

beginner_explanation: James's name for the single basic 'stuff' the whole world is made of, before it gets sorted into 'mind' and 'matter.'
academic_explanation: Defined by James as 'the immediate flux of life which furnishes the material to our later reflection'; the single primal stuff of radical empiricism, out of which the subject-object relation derivatively arises.

beginner_explanation: In Catholic doctrine, a state after death where souls are purified before entering heaven -- and which could supposedly be shortened by masses said for the dead. Protestants abolished the idea.
academic_explanation: The Catholic doctrine of an intermediate post-mortem state of purification from which souls could be delivered more quickly through masses and prayers; its abolition by Luther and Calvin removed both a theological claim and an associated ecclesiastical revenue stream.
related_concepts: The paradoxical weakening of clerical power by Protestant theology

beginner_explanation: The special, perfect substance Aristotle believed made up the stars and heavens, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire.
academic_explanation: The fifth element of On the Heavens, composing the supralunary region, whose sole natural motion is uniform circular rotation, in contrast to the rectilinear natural motions of the four terrestrial elements.
related_concepts: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)

beginner_explanation: James's view that the split between 'the mind that knows' and 'the object known' isn't basic to reality -- there's just one kind of raw material, experience, that can play either role.
academic_explanation: James's 1904 doctrine denying that the subject-object relation is fundamental, holding instead that there is only one primal stuff ('pure experience') out of which both knowers and known objects are constituted, knowing being a derivative relation between two portions of that stuff.

beginner_explanation: The other nineteenth-century current of rebellion against tradition, which stayed loyal to reasoned argument and eventually science, running from the French Revolution's philosophers through the English utilitarians to Marx.
academic_explanation: The current of revolt against eighteenth-century tradition that begins with the French Revolutionary philosophers, is transmitted in a more moderate, empirically detailed form by the English philosophical radicals, and reaches a 'deeper form' in Marx, issuing politically in Soviet Russia.

beginner_explanation: The view that general categories like 'cat' or 'man' are real things in their own right, not just names.
academic_explanation: The scholastic position, associated with William of Champeaux, that universals possess a mind-independent reality distinct from, and prior to, the particular things that instantiate them.

beginner_explanation: The correct scientific idea that the moon does not produce its own light but shines because it reflects sunlight.
academic_explanation: A doctrine Russell credits Anaxagoras with first clearly explaining, alongside the correct theory of eclipses and the knowledge that the moon lies below the sun.

beginner_explanation: Noticing your own mind at work -- thinking, doubting, believing -- as a second source of ideas alongside the five senses.
academic_explanation: Locke's second source of simple ideas, alongside sensation: perception of the operations of one's own mind.

beginner_explanation: The five perfectly symmetrical 3D shapes (cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron) that Plato links to the elements and the universe.
academic_explanation: The five convex polyhedra with congruent regular polygonal faces and equal angles, proven to be exactly five in number by Theaetetus, used by Timaeus to give the four sensible elements (plus the cosmos as a whole) a geometric structure.
related_concepts: The four elements and geometric atomism

beginner_explanation: The view that truth or morality is not fixed and universal but depends on the perspective of the individual or culture holding it.
academic_explanation: The philosophical position, exemplified by Protagoras, that truth-claims (or moral claims) lack an objective, perspective-independent grounding and are instead relative to the perceiver or the community.
related_concepts: 'Man is the measure of all things' (Protagorean relativism)

beginner_explanation: The idea that whether something is 'moving' only makes sense relative to something else -- there's no absolute fact about which of two things is really moving.
academic_explanation: The principle, incompatible with Aristotle's definition of motion as actualization of potential, that locomotion can only be meaningfully described relative to a chosen reference body, since if A moves relative to B, B equally moves relative to A.
related_concepts: Motion as the actualization of potential

beginner_explanation: The 'rebirth' of interest in classical Greek and Roman culture that began in fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Italy, marking the transition from the medieval to the modern outlook.
academic_explanation: The Italian cultural movement, beginning with individuals like Petrarch and spreading broadly by the fifteenth century, characterized by renewed direct engagement with classical antiquity, the partial substitution of ancient for ecclesiastical authority, and (per Russell) significant achievement in art and literature but not in original philosophy.
related_concepts: Substitution of the authority of the ancients for the authority of the Church

beginner_explanation: A nineteenth-century current of thought that valued passion, will, and dramatic individual self-assertion over calm reasoning, and that Russell traces from the poet Byron through the philosophers Schopenhauer and Nietzsche toward twentieth-century fascism.
academic_explanation: One of two currents of revolt against eighteenth-century tradition identified by Russell, emphasizing will over intellect, impatience with chains of reasoning, and glorification of certain forms of violence; allied historically with nationalism and, in Russell's genealogy, with Fascism.

beginner_explanation: The idea that only people who have gone through special training or discipline can really understand the deepest truths.
academic_explanation: A quasi-religious model, traced by Russell to the Pythagoreans, in which core truths are incommunicable except through a disciplined way of life, restricting genuine understanding (and, in Plato's case, political authority) to an initiated few.

beginner_explanation: A Jewish religious-political group, prominent among the priestly aristocracy, that rejected belief in an afterlife.
academic_explanation: A Jewish sect, largely drawn from the priestly and aristocratic class, that rejected the doctrine of personal immortality even after it had become widespread among other Jews by the time of Christ.

beginner_explanation: A pose of self-identification with Satan or with great sinners, used by Byron to convert his Calvinist sense of predestined wickedness into a source of grandeur rather than despair.
academic_explanation: The religious form Russell attributes to the aristocratic rebel's cosmic self-assertion in those, like Byron, who retain some superstition: identification with figures like Cain, Manfred, or Satan himself as an expression of proud, predestined transgression.

beginner_explanation: The philosophical position that certain knowledge is impossible, so the wise response is to suspend judgment about how things really are, while still going along with ordinary customs in practice.
academic_explanation: The school founded by Pyrrho, holding that no rational grounds exist for preferring one belief or course of action to another, extending traditional Greek doubts about sense-perception into a general doubt about ethics and logic, while distinguishing valid claims about how things 'appear' from unwarranted claims about how things objectively 'are.'

beginner_explanation: Machiavelli's idea that studying what actually makes political action succeed can be done objectively, the same way one might study any other practical skill, without judging whether the goal itself is good.
academic_explanation: Russell's characterization of Machiavelli's core methodological innovation: the study of effective political means as a value-neutral science, applicable equally to good and bad ends, distinguished from the separate question of the goodness of the ends pursued.
related_concepts: Machiavelli's separation of means from ends (the 'science of success')

beginner_explanation: Properties like colour, sound, and taste that Locke thought exist only in the mind of the perceiver, not in objects themselves.
academic_explanation: All perceivable qualities other than the primary ones -- colour, sound, smell, taste, etc. -- which Locke holds are 'only in the percipient.'

beginner_explanation: A prized capacity for strong, spontaneous emotion, especially sympathy, that Rousseau's contemporaries valued highly and that Rousseau embodied and promoted despite his often unkind actions.
academic_explanation: The eighteenth-century French cultural ideal of direct, uninformed emotional responsiveness that, per Russell, functioned in Rousseau's own ethic as a substitute for the ordinary virtues.

beginner_explanation: An eighteenth-century fashion for showing strong, immediate emotion, especially sympathy for the suffering of others -- prized for being spontaneous rather than reasoned.
academic_explanation: A cultivated eighteenth-century French disposition toward direct, uninformed emotional response, particularly sympathy, later given wider cultural and ethical significance by Rousseau as the basis of both his ethics and his theology.

beginner_explanation: The properties we actually perceive through our senses -- colours, sounds, tastes, textures -- as opposed to some hidden 'thing' supposedly behind them.
academic_explanation: The immediate objects of sense perception (colour, sound, taste, etc.), which Berkeley and Russell agree are what we actually perceive, rather than any underlying material substance.

beginner_explanation: An ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, made for Greek-speaking Jews.
academic_explanation: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures produced in Alexandria beginning in the mid-third century B.C. (the Pentateuch first), later relied upon heavily by early (mostly non-Hebrew-reading) Christians, though later shown by scholarship to differ significantly from the Hebrew original.

beginner_explanation: A scholastic term for the specific matter that makes a particular thing this individual thing rather than another of the same kind.
academic_explanation: In scholastic terminology, matter as marked out or individuated by specific quantitative dimensions, invoked in the objection that an immaterial being (like God) cannot know particulars, since particularity is constituted by signate matter.

beginner_explanation: The sin or crime of buying or selling positions or favors within the Church.
academic_explanation: The corrupt practice of purchasing ecclesiastical office or preferment, which Russell notes was rife in Gregory's time and remained a persistent problem until the later eleventh century.
related_concepts: Papal political authority under Gregory the Great
Simony and the campaign against it

beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's name for the morality of pity, humility, and equality he associates with Christianity and democracy, which he claims was invented by the weak to control and tame the strong.
academic_explanation: Nietzsche's genealogical category for a morality he attributes to resentment among the weak ('the bungled and botched'), which elevates values like compassion and equality precisely because they check and morally discredit the power of the strong.

beginner_explanation: The idea that government is legitimate only because people have agreed, implicitly or explicitly, to form a political community together.
academic_explanation: The doctrine that civil government originates in, and derives its authority from, the consent of those governed, who agree to leave the state of nature and form 'one body politic.'

beginner_explanation: An agreement by which people leave the state of nature and form a government -- in Hobbes's version, an agreement among the people themselves to obey whichever sovereign the majority chooses, not a deal between the people and the ruler.
academic_explanation: In Hobbes, a covenant made by citizens with one another (not with the sovereign) to obey the ruling power chosen by the majority, creating the 'Leviathan' or Commonwealth as an artificial person; treated by Russell as an 'explanatory myth' rather than a claimed historical event, and explicitly contrasted with the citizen-ruler covenants of Locke and Rousseau.
related_concepts: The social contract and the creation of 'Leviathan'

beginner_explanation: Russell's label (half-joking) for the other branch of post-Kantian liberal thought that, he schematically suggests, led eventually toward Hitler.
academic_explanation: Russell's schematic characterization of the liberal line running through Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, and Nietzsche.

beginner_explanation: The view that we can only really be sure of our own mind and experiences, not of other people's minds or an outside world.
academic_explanation: In Russell's taxonomy, the position allowing inference from present percepts only to other events within one's own biography, denying justified inference to other minds or to events no one perceives.

beginner_explanation: A paid, traveling teacher in ancient Greece who taught practical skills, especially persuasive speaking and argument, to young men who could afford it.
academic_explanation: Originally a neutral term roughly equivalent to 'professor,' denoting a professional teacher, typically without a fixed school or esoteric doctrine, who taught for a fee skills (chiefly rhetoric and argument) useful in law-courts and political life; the term later acquired a negative connotation largely through Plato's polemics.
related_concepts: The Sophists as a social and professional class

beginner_explanation: Traveling teachers in fifth-century Greece who taught young men skills such as persuasive argument, often for a fee.
academic_explanation: A class of professional itinerant teachers, sought after in Athens by young men wishing to learn the art of disputation; Plato's Protagoras satirizes their eager disciples.

beginner_explanation: The idea that the soul and body are two completely different kinds of thing, with the soul being the higher, more real of the two.
academic_explanation: Plato's metaphysical pairing of soul with reason/Ideas/reality and body with sense-perception/appearance/change, with death defined as their separation.

beginner_explanation: Hobbes's term for the hypothetical condition of human life before any government exists -- a constant, all-against-all struggle for self-preservation and dominance, with no property, law, or justice.
academic_explanation: In Hobbes's Leviathan, the pre-political condition in which naturally equal individuals, each driven by self-preservation to seek both liberty and dominion over others, are in perpetual conflict ('war of all against all'), lacking property, justice, or injustice, and governed only by 'force and fraud.'
related_concepts: Materialism and the state of nature as a 'war of all against all'

beginner_explanation: A calm, untroubled state with no unmet desires and no pain -- the goal of Epicurean life, rather than intense excitement or gratification.
academic_explanation: The equilibrium state Epicurus identified as the safest and truest form of pleasure, arising from the absence of unsatisfied desire and pain, as opposed to 'dynamic' pleasure, which depends on and follows a preceding painful want.

beginner_explanation: Things like health, wealth, and reputation, which Stoics said are neither truly good nor truly bad, because only virtue is truly good.
academic_explanation: In Stoic ethics, all things other than virtue and vice (health, wealth, pleasure, pain, life, death, reputation) are classified as 'indifferent' (adiaphora) to the sage's true good, though some may still be rationally 'preferred' or 'dispreferred' in ordinary conduct.

term: Struggle for existence / survival of the fittest
beginner_explanation: Darwin's idea that because more living things are born than can survive, those individuals whose traits happen to suit their environment best are more likely to live long enough to reproduce, gradually changing species over time.
academic_explanation: The mechanism of natural selection proposed by Darwin as the cause of evolution: given chance variation among offspring and competition for limited resources, favourable variations preponderate among survivors across generations, an idea Russell traces to Malthus's theory of population.

beginner_explanation: Latin for 'under the aspect of eternity' - looking at events as timeless facts rather than as things happening 'now' versus 'then.'
academic_explanation: Spinoza's ideal standpoint of reason, which views all events as part of the eternal, necessary order rather than privileging present or future over past.

beginner_explanation: The tendency in philosophy to treat one's own mind, experience, or point of view as the most certain starting point for knowledge, rather than the external world.
academic_explanation: Russell's term for the individualistic epistemological orientation, originating with Descartes's cogito, in which certainty about one's own thought is prioritized over, and used as the basis for inferring, knowledge of the external world -- a tendency he traces through Leibniz, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume into Kant, Fichte, and Rousseau.
related_concepts: Subjectivism as the recurring character of modern philosophy

beginner_explanation: The 'below the moon' region, where things are born and decay, versus the 'above the moon' region, where things (Aristotle believed) never change.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's cosmological division, in On the Heavens, between the corruptible, four-element terrestrial region below the moon and the eternal, incorruptible, fifth-element celestial region from the moon outward.
related_concepts: Sublunary versus supralunary cosmology (the fifth element)

beginner_explanation: The idea of a persisting 'thing' that underlies and owns its changing properties, like the 'real' Mr. Smith beneath everything he does and experiences.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's category (Categories) of an individual thing not predicable of, nor present in, any subject, taken by Russell to be a metaphysical illusion generated by the subject-predicate structure of ordinary sentences, rather than a genuine feature of reality.

beginner_explanation: What a proper name like 'Socrates' picks out: a particular, individual thing, as opposed to a general quality it might have.
academic_explanation: In Aristotle's primary sense, an individual thing that is neither predicable of, nor present in, a subject; a 'this' rather than a 'such,' contrasted with universals, which are common to many things.

beginner_explanation: The idea that behind all the changing properties of a thing, there is some underlying 'it' that stays the same and has those properties.
academic_explanation: The persistent subject of varying predicates; a concept Russell says later philosophy accepted from Parmenides in a moderated form, replacing his outright denial of change, and which remained central to philosophy, psychology, physics, and theology for over two thousand years.

beginner_explanation: The idea that nothing happens without some reason or explanation for why it is so and not otherwise.
academic_explanation: Leibniz's principle that every true proposition has a reason why it is true; in his published works, applied to contingent truths as motivating rather than logically necessitating; in his esoteric doctrine, held to mean that every true proposition is ultimately analytic.

beginner_explanation: A member of a mystical branch of Islam that sought direct, personal, often allegorical experience of religious truth.
academic_explanation: An adherent of Sufism, a mystical current within Islam, strong especially in Persia, that allowed itself wide latitude in mystical and allegorical interpretation of orthodox dogma; Russell describes it as 'more or less Neoplatonic.'

beginner_explanation: Aquinas's major work (1259-64) arguing for the truth of Christianity using reasons that do not presuppose the reader already accepts Christian revelation.
academic_explanation: A four-book systematic work by Aquinas addressed to an imagined reader versed in Arabic philosophy but not already Christian; the first three books rely on natural reason, while the fourth treats doctrines (Trinity, Incarnation, sacraments, resurrection) knowable only through revelation.

beginner_explanation: A three-part logical argument with a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion, like 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.'
academic_explanation: Aristotle's central deductive form, classified by the scholastics into named figures and moods (e.g., Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio in the first figure), long treated as the exhaustive model of valid deductive inference.

beginner_explanation: A statement that tells you something new about the world (not just true by definition) but that you can know for certain without needing to check by experience -- Kant's example is arithmetic and geometry.
academic_explanation: A judgement whose predicate is not contained in its subject (synthetic) yet which is known independently of experience (a priori); Kant's central question is how such judgements, exemplified by mathematics and the law of causality, are possible.

beginner_explanation: Locke's image for the mind before any experience: a blank sheet with nothing written on it.
academic_explanation: The doctrine that the mind, prior to experience, has no innate ideas or principles, and is furnished entirely by sensation and reflection.

beginner_explanation: The idea, taken from Locke and pushed to an extreme by Helvétius, that people are born as 'blank slates' with no fixed talents or character, so that everything about an adult's mind and virtue is the product of upbringing.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, associated with Locke and radicalized by Helvétius, that individual differences in talent and virtue arise wholly from differences in education and social/political circumstance rather than from any congenital or innate endowment.

beginner_explanation: Explaining something by the purpose it serves, rather than by mechanical cause and effect.
academic_explanation: An explanatory mode that accounts for phenomena in terms of ends or purposes ('the Good') rather than efficient/mechanical causes; Russell attributes Plato's preference for this mode to Socrates's influence.

beginner_explanation: Explaining something by the purpose or goal it serves, rather than by what caused it.
academic_explanation: An explanation by final cause: an event in the future for the sake of which an occurrence takes place; Russell associates this method with Socrates, Plato, and especially Aristotle, in contrast to the atomists' mechanistic method.

beginner_explanation: Occam's distinction between words that point directly at things in the world (first intention) and words that point at other words or concepts (second intention).
academic_explanation: In Occam's logic, terms of first intention signify things directly and belong to the sciences; terms of second intention signify other terms/concepts and belong to logic; confusing the two produces fallacies such as 'Socrates is a species.'
related_concepts: Occam's separation of logic from metaphysics and theology

beginner_explanation: Origen's idea that Christians' true political loyalty belongs to the Church, not to the secular (pagan) state.
academic_explanation: Origen's doctrine that Christians should not participate in the government of the State but only of the Church, understood as the true 'divine nation' -- an early formulation of the Church/State dualism developed further in Saint Augustine's City of God.

beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's ideal aristocratic type: capable of cruelty when necessary, recognizing duties only to equals, and embodying strength of will rather than sympathy or humility.
academic_explanation: Nietzsche's positive ethical ideal, replacing the Christian saint: a governing-aristocrat type who recognizes duties only toward equals, protects and patronizes artists and skilled craftsmen from a position of superiority, and is essentially defined as the incarnate will to power.

beginner_explanation: Hegel's name for the single, fully real Whole of the universe, of which individual things are only partial, dependent aspects.
academic_explanation: The complex, organically unified, spiritual Whole that alone possesses complete reality in Hegel's system; finite things have degrees of reality only insofar as they are correctly seen as aspects of it.

beginner_explanation: Saint Benedict's written guidelines for how monks should live together, including strong authority for the abbot and moderate (not extreme) austerity.
academic_explanation: The monastic rule composed by Saint Benedict around 520 at Monte Cassino, which became the governing template for nearly all Western monasteries outside Ireland.

beginner_explanation: Anaximander's name for the basic 'stuff' of the universe: something infinite, eternal, and unlike any of the ordinary substances we know (not water, not air, not fire).
academic_explanation: Anaximander's term for the indeterminate, infinite, and ageless primal substance from which the known opposed elements are differentiated and into which they eventually return, in accordance with cosmic 'justice'.

beginner_explanation: A romantic character type -- proud, rebellious, and often violent or self-destructive -- who defies social convention and morality.
academic_explanation: The type of man Russell says is 'encouraged by romanticism, especially of the Byronic variety': violent and anti-social, appearing either as an anarchic rebel or as a conquering tyrant.

beginner_explanation: Twelve basic mental 'filing categories' (like unity, cause-and-effect, existence) that Kant says the mind automatically applies to organize any experience.
academic_explanation: Twelve a priori concepts derived by Kant from the forms of the syllogism, divided into quantity, quality, relation, and modality, applicable to all phenomena but not, on Kant's view, to things-in-themselves.
related_concepts: Space and time as a priori forms of intuition

beginner_explanation: The belief that God picked out one group for special favor and a special role in history.
academic_explanation: The doctrine of divine election of a specific people (Israel) or, in Christian adaptation, a specific community ('the elect') as objects of God's particular love and salvific purpose.

beginner_explanation: Augustine's name for the community of the elect, the true, invisible society of the saved, as opposed to the ordinary earthly societies of this world.
academic_explanation: In Augustine's philosophy of history, the pilgrim society of the predestined elect, commingled in this life with the earthly city but destined to be eternally separated from it at the Last Judgement.

beginner_explanation: Empedocles' idea that everything is made from just four basic, everlasting ingredients: earth, air, fire, and water, mixed in different amounts.
academic_explanation: Empedocles' doctrine that earth, air, fire, and water are each eternal and unchanging, combined and separated by Love and Strife to produce the world's changing compound substances; the standard theory of matter in antiquity until early chemistry.

beginner_explanation: The highest Idea in Plato's system, compared to the sun: it makes both reality and the ability to know reality possible.
academic_explanation: The Idea that, in Plato's scheme, 'far exceeds essence in dignity and power,' serving as both the source of the reality of the other Ideas and the source of the mind's capacity to know them.
related_concepts: The divided line: Reason versus Understanding

beginner_explanation: A Catholic religious order founded by Ignatius of Loyola, organized like an army, dedicated to fighting heresy through education, missionary work, and disciplined obedience -- the main force behind the Counter-Reformation's success.
academic_explanation: The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola on quasi-military lines of strict obedience to the General, influential from the Council of Trent onward through disciplined propaganda, missionary expansion (notably in the Far East), skillful practice as confessors, and dominance of European education; theologically opposed to predestination, affirming free will and salvation by faith and works.
related_concepts: The Jesuit method: discipline, education, and missionary zeal

beginner_explanation: The body of religious rules -- like keeping the Sabbath, avoiding certain foods, and circumcision -- that mark someone as Jewish.
academic_explanation: The Mosaic Law (Torah), comprising ethical, ceremonial, and ritual precepts, which took on heightened importance as a marker of national-religious identity during and after the Babylonian exile.

beginner_explanation: Plotinus's name for the single, ultimate source of all reality -- so far beyond ordinary description that almost nothing can truthfully be said about it except that it exists.
academic_explanation: In Plotinus's metaphysics, the first and highest hypostasis: an utterly simple, transcendent source of all reality, beyond Being, beyond even 'the Good' and 'the Beautiful' as ordinarily conceived, of which no predicates can properly be affirmed beyond the bare assertion 'It is.'

beginner_explanation: Parmenides' name for the single, unchanging thing he believed is the only real thing in the universe, behind the illusion of many changing things.
academic_explanation: The sole reality in Parmenides' metaphysics: infinite and indivisible being, conceived as extended (even sphere-like) yet without genuine internal division or opposition, since Parmenides denies that 'opposites' like hot and cold are anything more than the presence or absence of one quality.

beginner_explanation: Erasmus's most famous book, a satire spoken in the voice of 'Folly' herself, mocking human vanity, professional conceit, and especially the corruption and hypocrisy of the Church, before ending with a serious suggestion that true religious faith is itself a kind of holy foolishness.
academic_explanation: Erasmus's 1509 satirical work (Encomium Moriae), delivered as an oration by the personification of Folly, combining ironic praise of human self-deception and vanity with fierce criticism of ecclesiastical abuses, and concluding with the serious argument that genuine Christian devotion is a form of 'folly' opposed to scholastic intellectualism.
related_concepts: True religion as 'holy folly': the rejection of theological system-building

beginner_explanation: The puzzle of why we're justified in assuming the future will be like the past, given that we can't prove this using either pure logic or past experience (without going in a circle).
academic_explanation: Hume's demonstration that the principle of the uniformity of nature -- required to justify inductive inference from observed to unobserved cases -- can be established neither a priori nor by any non-circular empirical argument.

beginner_explanation: A strange third category, besides unchanging Ideas and changing physical things, that Plato says provides the 'place' or 'home' in which physical things exist.
academic_explanation: Timaeus's proposed third kind of being -- eternal like the Forms but providing a home for sensible becoming -- apprehended only by a 'kind of spurious reason,' which Russell finds obscure but compares to Kant's later account of space.

term: The saint by nature vs. the saint from fear
beginner_explanation: Russell's distinction between someone who is genuinely, spontaneously kind because it makes them happy, and someone who only avoids wrongdoing because they fear punishment (from God, hell, or their neighbors).
academic_explanation: Russell's critical distinction, introduced to diagnose a limit in Nietzsche's psychology: Nietzsche, being full of fear and hatred, can only conceive of virtue as fear-motivated restraint ('the saint from fear'), and cannot imagine spontaneous, fearless, non-self-interested love as a real possibility ('the saint by nature').

beginner_explanation: Rousseau's idea that people form society by each giving up all their individual rights completely and equally to the community as a whole, so no one person rules over another.
academic_explanation: The total, unreserved alienation of each associate's person and rights to the whole community, creating a moral and collective body called the State (passive), the Sovereign (active), or a Power (in relation to other such bodies).

beginner_explanation: The puzzle of figuring out what the real Socrates was actually like, since we only know him through other people's writings.
academic_explanation: The historiographical difficulty of reconstructing the historical Socrates from the divergent, non-neutral testimonies of Xenophon and Plato.

beginner_explanation: The idealized, often inaccurate legend of Sparta that later writers admired and imitated.
academic_explanation: The romanticized account of Spartan institutions, chiefly transmitted by Plutarch's Life of Lycurgus, which Russell argues had greater historical influence on political thought (via Plato, Rousseau, Nietzsche, and National Socialism) than the documented Spartan reality.

beginner_explanation: Truly empty space, with nothing at all in it, which the atomists said must exist so that atoms have room to move.
academic_explanation: Empty space, treated by the atomists as a form of not-being that nonetheless must exist to make motion possible, in direct defiance of Parmenides's argument that not-being cannot be said to exist.
related_concepts: The void as a response to Parmenides

beginner_explanation: The Greek root of our word 'theory', originally meaning passionate, quasi-religious contemplation, later redirected by Pythagoras toward intellectual and mathematical contemplation.
academic_explanation: Originally an Orphic term for ecstatic, sympathetic identification with a suffering god; transformed by Pythagoras into disinterested intellectual contemplation, understood as the highest form of purification and the origin of the modern sense of 'theory'.

beginner_explanation: Russell's technique for showing that phrases like 'the golden mountain' don't actually name anything -- once you spell out what such sentences really mean, the phrase disappears.
academic_explanation: Russell's analysis of sentences containing a definite description ('the so-and-so'), on which the phrase is eliminated in favour of an existence-and-uniqueness claim, resolving puzzles about nonexistent objects and clarifying that 'existence' can only be predicated of descriptions, not of names.

beginner_explanation: A short 1845 text by Marx arguing that philosophy's real job is to change the world, not just interpret it.
academic_explanation: Marx's eleven theses (1845) criticizing Feuerbach's contemplative materialism and asserting that the reality and power of thought must be demonstrated in practice, culminating in the claim that 'philosophers have only interpreted the world... the real task is to alter it.'

beginner_explanation: A brutal massacre of thousands of civilians ordered by Emperor Theodosius in revenge for a riot, for which Ambrose forced him to do public penance.
academic_explanation: The A.D. 390 massacre of several thousand people in Thessalonica ordered by Theodosius in retaliation for the murder of a garrison commander; Ambrose's subsequent refusal to allow Theodosius to receive communion until he performed public penance is presented by Russell as Ambrose's most morally admirable act, independent of Church-power politics.
related_concepts: Independence of the Church from the State

beginner_explanation: The unknowable 'real' object that supposedly causes our sensations, as opposed to the object as it appears to us.
academic_explanation: In Kant's system, the noumenal reality underlying phenomena, not situated in space or time and not describable by the categories, yet treated (inconsistently, per Russell) as a cause of sensation.

beginner_explanation: Kant's idea of the unknowable reality behind appearances; while Fichte and Hegel dropped this idea, Schopenhauer kept it and claimed it is, in fact, Will.
academic_explanation: Kant's noumenal reality underlying phenomena, which Schopenhauer -- unlike Fichte and Hegel, who abandoned it -- retains and identifies with Will, arguing the body is merely its phenomenal appearance.

beginner_explanation: A logical puzzle: if a thing resembles its Idea, you'd need another Idea to explain that resemblance, and then another, forever.
academic_explanation: The regress objection, raised by Parmenides against Socrates and later independently by Aristotle, showing that participation-by-resemblance between particular and Idea generates an infinite series of further Ideas.

beginner_explanation: A brief, harsh group of thirty rulers who took power in Athens with Spartan help after the Peloponnesian War.
academic_explanation: The short-lived oligarchic government (404-403 B.C.) installed in Athens after its defeat by Sparta, led by Critias, a former associate of Socrates, whose excesses shadowed Socrates's later prosecution.

beginner_explanation: The claim that 'justice' really just means whatever benefits whoever is in power.
academic_explanation: The position, voiced by the Sophist Thrasymachus in Republic Book I, that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger, challenging any claim to an objective, power-independent standard of right and wrong.

beginner_explanation: The idea that after death, souls are reborn into new bodies -- human or animal -- depending on how they lived.
academic_explanation: The Orphic-Pythagorean doctrine, adopted by Plato, that impure or merely virtuous (non-philosophic) souls are reborn into human or animal bodies fitting their moral character, while purified philosophic souls dwell with the gods.
related_concepts: Transmigration and the fate of souls

beginner_explanation: The idea that after death, souls are reborn as women, birds, land animals, or fish, depending on how virtuously or wisely they lived.
academic_explanation: Timaeus's account of post-mortem rebirth, in which moral and intellectual failure in one incarnation determines a progressively lower form of embodiment in the next, continuous with the Phaedo's Orphic-Pythagorean doctrine.

beginner_explanation: The belief that after death, a soul is reborn in a new body -- possibly even an animal's -- and this cycle repeats many times.
academic_explanation: The Pythagorean (and Orphic) doctrine that the soul is immortal and passes through successive incarnations, its progress toward purification or its degree of pollution determining the nature of each subsequent embodiment.

beginner_explanation: The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of communion actually become the body and blood of Christ.
academic_explanation: The Catholic sacramental doctrine that in the Eucharist the substance of bread and wine is converted into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the accidents (appearance) remain unchanged; Wycliffe's outright denial of this doctrine marked his final and most decisive break with orthodoxy.

beginner_explanation: The Greek goddess of luck or chance, worshipped increasingly as ordinary life came to feel unpredictable and uncontrollable.
academic_explanation: The personification of arbitrary chance in Hellenistic religion, whose growing cult Russell reads as a symptom of the era's political and economic insecurity, existing in uneasy coexistence with the competing belief in astrological necessity.

beginner_explanation: A general word or quality, like 'man' or 'white,' that can apply to many different particular things.
academic_explanation: That which is 'of such a nature as to be predicated of many subjects'; Aristotle denies universals are themselves substances, since substance must be peculiar to one thing.

beginner_explanation: The Heraclitean idea that absolutely everything is constantly changing, in every respect, all the time.
academic_explanation: The doctrine, radicalized by Heraclitus's Ephesian disciples in the Theaetetus, that a thing changes both in place and in every quality without cessation, which Plato shows destroys the fixity of meaning needed for any coherent assertion.

beginner_explanation: Newton's law that every object in the universe pulls on every other object, with a strength that depends on how massive they are and how far apart they are.
academic_explanation: Newton's law that every body attracts every other body with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, derived from showing that Kepler's three laws are equivalent to a specific inverse-square acceleration toward the sun.
related_concepts: Newton's law of universal gravitation and the unification of celestial and terrestrial mechanics

beginner_explanation: The idea that every tiny bit of matter contains a little of everything, not just one pure substance.
academic_explanation: Anaxagoras's doctrine that matter is infinitely divisible and every portion, however small, contains some share of every element except mind; things are named for the element that predominates in them.
related_concepts: Universal mixture / infinite divisibility of matter

beginner_explanation: Latin terms for 'universal before the thing' (an idea in God's mind before creation) and 'universal after the thing' (a general concept formed in the human mind after experiencing many particular things).
academic_explanation: Scholastic terms (introduced fully in Chapter X via Avicenna) distinguishing universals as they exist in the divine mind prior to creation from universals as abstracted human concepts; Occam accepts the former only for explaining creation, not for explaining ordinary human knowledge, where only the post rem sense applies.

beginner_explanation: Aristotle's God: an eternal being that causes all motion in the universe without itself ever moving, by being the object of love and desire rather than by pushing things.
academic_explanation: Aristotle's First Cause: an eternal, immaterial substance, pure form and pure actuality, that causes motion as a final cause; identified with self-contemplating divine thought, 'a thinking on thinking.'
related_concepts: The unmoved mover and circular motion

beginner_explanation: Lending money at interest, which Aristotle condemned as the most unnatural way to make money.
academic_explanation: In Aristotle's usage, any lending of money at interest (not only exorbitant rates, as in later usage), condemned as unnatural because it generates a gain from money itself rather than from money's proper function as a medium of exchange.

beginner_explanation: The ethical view that the right action or policy is whichever one produces the greatest balance of happiness over unhappiness for everyone affected.
academic_explanation: Bentham's doctrine that pleasure and pain are the sole measures of good and evil, and that the best state of affairs is the one containing the greatest net balance of pleasure over pain, summed across all affected persons.

beginner_explanation: Thomas More's 1518 book describing an imaginary island society with communal property, equality, and rational planning of daily life -- the origin of the word 'utopian.'
academic_explanation: More's 1518 work, modeled on Plato's Republic, presenting (through the fictional traveler Raphael Hythloday) a communist island society without private property, characterized by egalitarian labor, religious toleration, opposition to capital punishment for theft, and rigid social uniformity, which Russell judges genuinely liberal in intent but ultimately incompatible with human happiness due to its lack of diversity.
related_concepts: More's Utopia: communism, equality, and rational social planning

beginner_explanation: A Hindu concept Schopenhauer adopts for the illusion that makes us see ourselves as separate from other people and things; seeing through it is the beginning of wisdom and compassion.
academic_explanation: Schopenhauer's term (borrowed from Hindu philosophy) for the illusion of individuation and separateness in the phenomenal world; the good man, through sympathetic insight, sees through this veil and recognizes the underlying unity of all suffering beings.

beginner_explanation: The idea that if you truly know what is good, you will automatically do it.
academic_explanation: The Socratic doctrine that no one sins knowingly, making knowledge of the good both necessary and sufficient for virtuous conduct.

beginner_explanation: Not moral 'virtue' in the ordinary sense, but skill, boldness, and effectiveness in gaining and using political power.
academic_explanation: Though Russell does not use the Italian term directly, the quality he describes -- admired skill and dexterity in political action, exemplified by Caesar Borgia, judged independently of the moral worth of the ends pursued -- corresponds to what is commonly called Machiavellian virtù in later scholarship.
related_concepts: The doctrine of The Prince: the ruler's necessary use of deception and force

beginner_explanation: Saint Jerome's Latin translation of the Bible, made mostly from the original Hebrew and Greek, which became the Catholic Church's standard Bible.
academic_explanation: Jerome's Latin translation of Scripture, notable for translating the Old Testament directly from Hebrew rather than via the Septuagint, initially controversial but eventually authoritative in the Western/Catholic Church.

beginner_explanation: Followers of Peter Waldo who gave up their possessions, preached poverty, and eventually rejected the authority of Catholic priests.
academic_explanation: A reformist religious movement founded by Peter Waldo around 1170, initially papally approved but condemned in 1184 after criticizing clerical immorality; they appointed their own ministers independent of the Catholic priesthood and spread to Lombardy and Bohemia, where they influenced the later Hussites.

beginner_explanation: Dewey's substitute for 'truth': a belief is justified to assert not because it matches a fixed fact, but because of how well the activities it inspires turn out.
academic_explanation: Dewey's term, used in place of 'truth,' for the status a belief acquires when the activities it inspires in an organism have satisfactory rather than unsatisfactory consequences; contrasted by Russell with a causally grounded notion of truth about the past.

beginner_explanation: A related idea developed by John Dewey, discussed in the next chapter, that substitutes for 'truth' the notion of a belief being justified by present evidence for future action.
academic_explanation: Not James's own term, but flagged here as the concept explored fully in the following chapter's contrast between James's and Dewey's versions of pragmatism.

term: Way of truth / way of opinion
beginner_explanation: The two parts of Parmenides' poem: one describing what is really, truly the case (the unchanging One), and one describing the deceptive world as it merely appears to the senses.
academic_explanation: Parmenides' division of his poem On Nature into 'the way of truth', concerning unchanging Being accessible to reason, and 'the way of opinion', concerning the illusory world of sensory appearance -- of which only the former survives in enough detail to reconstruct.

beginner_explanation: James's claim that when evidence can't settle a big, unavoidable question (like religion), we're entitled to just choose to believe.
academic_explanation: James's 1896 doctrine that the duty of veracity comprises two coequal precepts ('believe truth' and 'shun error'), licensing a believing attitude in forced, momentous, evidentially undecidable options even without intellectual coercion by evidence.

beginner_explanation: Nietzsche's idea that the deepest human drive is not pleasure or survival but the desire for power -- the capacity to overcome resistance and impose one's will.
academic_explanation: Nietzsche's central psychological/ethical category, treating power (measured by the resistance a will can overcome and the suffering it can endure and use to its advantage) as the fundamental measure of vitality and value.

beginner_explanation: The name of the God of Israel in the Hebrew Bible.
academic_explanation: The tetragrammaton-derived name for the Israelite deity, originally, per Russell's account, one tribal god among several regional gods before becoming, through prophetic reinterpretation, the sole God.
